source: Rick Hightower (Intent Solutions team, first cohort member to pass CCA-F). Original scenario-based practice questions authored for CCA-F study; reuse granted by Rick + Jeremy 2026-07-21. Deduped across his practice-exam set. Not reproduced from Anthropic's exam.
note: answerIndex refers to the option's 0-based POSITION in the options array.

questions.text: Your coordinator delegates a literature review task to the document analysis subagent. The coordinator's system prompt specifies that all citations must follow IEEE format, but the subagent returns results with APA citations. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The subagent's underlying model does not support IEEE citation formatting
The IEEE format requirement existed in the coordinator's context but was never explicitly included in the task delegation message
Citation formatting is a runtime feature that requires a separate tool call
The coordinator should have used few-shot examples in its own system prompt
questions.rationale: Subagents do NOT inherit the coordinator's context. They start with a blank slate and see only what was explicitly forwarded in the delegation message. The IEEE format requirement was in the coordinator's context but was never explicitly passed through, so the subagent had no way to know about it. This is the canonical context isolation question on the CCA exam.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A teammate suggests letting the data extraction subagent send its results directly to the report writer subagent to skip a coordinator step. Why is the hub-and-spoke pattern preferable?
options: Direct subagent-to-subagent communication is technically impossible in the Agent SDK
The coordinator can observe all interactions, apply consistent error handling, and control what information each subagent receives
Hub-and-spoke is faster because it reduces network hops
Subagent-to-subagent communication requires expensive MCP server configuration
questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke centralizes visibility into all interactions, ensures consistent error handling across the system, and gives the coordinator fine-grained control over what each subagent receives. Direct subagent-to-subagent communication breaks observability and makes coordinated recovery much harder.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Production logs show that requests like 'pull recent academic papers on lithium battery degradation' are misrouted: sometimes the document analysis tool is called with a search query, sometimes the web search tool is called with a PDF URL. Both tools have descriptions that mention 'analyzing content from sources.' What is the most effective fix?
options: Add few-shot examples to the coordinator's system prompt for each routing pattern
Add a third disambiguation tool that asks the coordinator which type of source it has
Rename and rewrite the descriptions so each tool clearly states its input type, output, and what it does NOT handle (with a pointer to the sibling tool)
Combine the two tools into one generic content_analyzer tool with a 'source_type' parameter
questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary routing mechanism. Semantic overlap between descriptions causes misrouting. The fix is to eliminate ambiguity at the source: rename tools to be purpose-specific and add negative bounds ('does NOT handle...'). Few-shot examples paper over the problem. Combining the tools loses distinct functionality.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The web search subagent times out after 30 seconds while researching an obscure topic. What is the most effective way for the subagent to report this failure back to the coordinator?
options: Return an empty result set so the coordinator can proceed without interruption
Return a generic 'search failed' string and let the coordinator decide whether to retry
Return structured error context including failure type (timeout), the attempted query, any partial results gathered, and possible alternative approaches
Retry silently until the search succeeds, regardless of how long it takes
questions.rationale: Structured error responses give the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions. Knowing it was a timeout (transient, likely retryable), what query was tried, any partial results, and possible alternatives lets the coordinator either retry with a narrower query, fall back to other sources, or proceed with what it has and annotate gaps.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: After running on the query 'evolution of remote work practices,' your final report covers only software engineering and tech startups. The web search subagent returned exactly what the coordinator asked for. The document analysis subagent returned exactly what the coordinator asked for. The synthesis agent integrated everything competently. Where is the bug?
options: The synthesis agent over-weighted certain sources
The subagents need more diverse tool access
The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow — it only delegated subtopics within tech, never sectors like healthcare, finance, education, or government
The coordinator should run the same query through additional subagents
questions.rationale: When every subagent executes correctly but the final output has coverage gaps, the bug is upstream in the coordinator's decomposition. The coordinator partitioned 'remote work' into tech-only subtopics, so the subagents never had a chance to cover other sectors. Fix the decomposition, not the subagents.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The document analysis subagent encounters a corrupted PDF it cannot parse. What is the best handling strategy?
options: Crash the entire pipeline so the user knows immediately that something went wrong
Return a structured error to the coordinator with file ID, error category, and what was attempted, letting the coordinator decide whether to skip, retry with an alternative parser, or escalate
Silently substitute synthetic content so the report writer has something to work with
Have the subagent attempt to repair the PDF using a different model
questions.rationale: Local-then-escalate is the pattern: the subagent reports the failure with full context (file ID, what was attempted, error category) and lets the coordinator make the recovery decision. The coordinator has the broader context to choose between skipping, retrying, or escalating. Crashing destroys partial progress; substitution introduces hallucinated data.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your coordinator dispatches web search and document analysis in parallel for the topic 'consumer drone regulations 2026.' Logs reveal both subagents are searching overlapping aspects: both pulled in FAA documents, both queried recent news. The redundant work doubled token usage. What is the best fix?
options: Run web search and document analysis sequentially instead of in parallel so the second one can avoid duplication
Add a deduplication pass after both finish to drop overlapping content
Have the coordinator explicitly partition the research space upfront, assigning distinct source types and subtopics to each subagent before any work begins
Reduce the maximum tokens for each subagent so they cannot return as much content
questions.rationale: Upfront partitioning preserves the speed of parallel execution while preventing duplicated effort. The coordinator decides 'web search handles news and blogs; document analysis handles FAA filings and academic papers' before delegation. Going sequential surrenders the parallelism benefit. Post-hoc deduplication wastes the tokens already spent.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You initially gave the synthesis subagent access to a general-purpose 'fetch_url' tool so it could occasionally pull supporting context. Production shows the synthesis agent now uses this tool for ad-hoc web searches by passing search engine URLs, drifting from its synthesis role. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Add a system prompt rule forbidding the synthesis agent from constructing search URLs
Replace fetch_url with a scoped 'load_reference_document' tool that validates URLs point to known document formats only
Move the synthesis agent behind a permission layer that rate-limits fetch_url
Train the synthesis agent with few-shot examples showing only synthesis behavior
questions.rationale: Constrain capability at the interface level (principle of least privilege). A scoped tool that only accepts document URLs makes the undesired search behavior structurally impossible, rather than merely discouraged by prose. Prompt-only restrictions are probabilistic; tool design is deterministic.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The synthesis agent receives aggregated input that's grown to 90K tokens. Quality is consistently strong on the first and last sections of its output but the middle sections are shallow, repeat earlier claims, or miss key facts that were buried halfway through the input. What is the most effective mitigation?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window
Place a 'key findings' summary at the top of the aggregated input, add explicit section headers throughout, and order the most important supporting evidence near the start and end
Increase the synthesis agent's max_tokens output limit
Lower the temperature setting on the synthesis agent
questions.rationale: This is the 'lost in the middle' effect. A larger context window does not change attention distribution — the same pattern reappears at a bigger scale. The fix is structural: prime with a summary at the top (primacy effect), use headers to give the model navigation anchors, and place the most important material at the edges of the context where attention is strongest.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The web search subagent and document analysis subagent have both finished. In the hub-and-spoke pattern, what happens next?
options: The two subagents negotiate which findings to forward to the synthesis agent
The coordinator receives both result sets and forwards them, with relevant context, to the synthesis subagent
The synthesis agent polls the other subagents for their outputs
Findings are written to a shared scratchpad that the synthesis agent reads
questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke means results flow back to the coordinator, which then routes them to the next stage. Subagents do not communicate directly. The coordinator owns visibility, error handling, and explicit context passing.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Combined input to the synthesis agent — web pages, full document text, chain-of-thought reasoning — is now 110K tokens and synthesis quality has degraded. What is the most effective root-cause fix?
options: Reduce the synthesis agent's max_tokens so it produces shorter output
Modify upstream subagents to return only structured findings (key facts, citations, relevance scores) instead of raw page content and reasoning chains
Use prompt caching on the synthesis agent's input
Split the synthesis agent across multiple sequential calls
questions.rationale: Address the volume at the source. If the synthesis agent only needs structured findings, give it structured findings. Verbose page content and reasoning traces inflate token counts without adding value. Prompt caching addresses cost, not quality. Smaller max_tokens shortens output but doesn't fix the polluted input.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The document analysis subagent encounters transient PDF parsing errors on roughly 8% of inputs that succeed on retry. Currently every failure escalates to the coordinator. The coordinator is now spending much of its time on document retries instead of orchestration. What is the best change?
options: Increase the coordinator's tokens so it can handle the retry traffic
Have the subagent implement local recovery for transient failures, only escalating to the coordinator the errors it could not resolve — along with what was attempted and any partial results
Disable retries entirely and skip files that fail on the first attempt
Replace the document analysis subagent with a more capable model
questions.rationale: Handle errors at the lowest level capable of resolving them. Transient errors should be retried within the subagent. Only escalate what cannot be resolved locally, and when escalating, include full context (what was attempted, partial results). This frees the coordinator to do its actual job.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Two credible peer-reviewed sources report different figures for global EV adoption in 2025: 22% and 17%. The document analysis subagent has to decide what to do. Which behavior aligns with the CCA exam's expectations?
options: Pick the higher figure since it's more likely to be the latest revision
Average the two values and forward 19.5% to synthesis
Complete the analysis with both figures retained, annotate the conflict with source attribution, and let the coordinator decide how (or whether) to reconcile before synthesis
Halt processing and ask the user to resolve the conflict before continuing
questions.rationale: Separation of concerns: the document analysis subagent's job is to analyze. Conflict resolution belongs to the coordinator, which has broader context. Preserving both values with source attribution is the disciplined choice. Averaging or arbitrarily picking discards information; blocking the pipeline on every conflict is brittle.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The web search subagent successfully queried 3 of 5 source categories. The other 2 timed out. How should the synthesis agent represent the final report?
options: Suppress mention of the missing categories so the report appears complete
Refuse to synthesize until all 5 categories return results
Structure the output with coverage annotations indicating which findings are well-supported and which topic areas have gaps due to unavailable sources
Re-delegate the work to a different subagent for the missing categories
questions.rationale: Graceful degradation with transparency: preserve the value of the work that succeeded, but propagate the uncertainty so downstream consumers can make informed decisions. Hiding the gaps damages trust; refusing to synthesize discards real value; mechanical re-delegation might just reproduce the same timeout.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Subagent logs show a patent database query returned '0 results' and a separate industry-report search timed out. The coordinator treats both as the same kind of failure and retries both. Why is this wrong?
options: Both should be silently dropped from the final report
Retrying a database query causes cost overruns
A timeout is an access failure that may benefit from a retry; '0 results' is a successful query with a valid empty result — they are semantically different outcomes that warrant different responses
The coordinator should batch all retries to save tokens
questions.rationale: 'No matches' is a valid, informative result. 'Timeout' is an access failure. Conflating them either wastes retries on legitimately empty queries or treats genuine failures as if they were complete. Structured error responses distinguish access failures from valid empty results.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Production logs reveal that for a multi-part request like 'cancel order #5582, refund my last membership charge, and update my shipping address,' your agent issues 11 tool calls including duplicate get_customer lookups and re-fetches the same customer profile three times before resolving each concern. Single-issue requests average 3 calls. What is the most effective restructuring?
options: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt for each multi-part scenario
Add a hard cap on total tool calls per resolution
Have the agent decompose the request into distinct concerns and investigate each in parallel using shared customer context, then synthesize a unified resolution
Force the agent to handle one concern per conversation turn
questions.rationale: The two structural problems are: (1) redundant context fetching across concerns and (2) sequential investigation. Decomposing the request, sharing customer context, and investigating concerns in parallel addresses both. Few-shot examples may help for known phrasings but won't systematically eliminate the redundancy.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your support agent averages 5 sequential API round-trips per resolution. Trace analysis shows that get_customer, lookup_order, and check_loyalty_status are each called in separate turns even when needed together. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Combine all three tools into a single 'get_customer_full_profile' tool
Prompt Claude to batch related tool calls in a single turn and return all tool results together before the next API call
Run the agent on a faster model to reduce per-call latency
Add caching middleware that pre-fetches customer data on every request
questions.rationale: Claude can request multiple tools in a single turn natively. Prompting it to batch related tool calls (and returning all results together) directly addresses the sequential pattern with no architectural changes. Combining tools loses specialization; the model speed addresses symptoms, not the redundant turn pattern.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Logs show the agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about their order status, even though lookup_order is the obviously correct tool. Both tools have minimal one-line descriptions. What is the first diagnostic step?
options: Switch to a different model with better tool-calling accuracy
Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks get_customer for order queries
Review and expand each tool's description so they clearly differentiate purpose, expected inputs, example queries, and when to use one over the other
Add a system prompt rule saying 'always use lookup_order for order questions'
questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary input the LLM uses to choose between tools. When selection is unreliable and descriptions are minimal, the first move is always to improve the descriptions. Programmatic blocking and model swaps treat symptoms; system-prompt rules can conflict with descriptions.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent resolves complex billing disputes with the right answer about 90% of the time, but the explanation it gives the customer is inconsistent — sometimes it cites the policy, sometimes it forgets to mention the timeline, sometimes it leaves out next steps. Manual review is too slow to scale. What is the best mitigation?
options: Switch to a more capable model for billing disputes
Add a self-critique step where the agent evaluates its own draft response against criteria (policy cited? timeline mentioned? next steps clear?) and revises before delivery
Have a human review every billing-dispute response
Lower temperature on the agent so it produces more consistent text
questions.rationale: Evaluator-optimizer pattern: the agent grades its own draft against explicit criteria and revises if anything is missing. This catches case-specific completeness gaps without requiring human review. Temperature affects randomness but not whether the agent remembers to include each required element.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your tool descriptions are already detailed and unambiguous, but logs reveal that whenever a customer's message contains the word 'subscription,' the agent reaches for get_customer instead of lookup_subscription_plan — even when 'subscription' refers to the plan, not the user. Resolution success drops from 92% to 76% on these messages. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The tool descriptions still have residual semantic overlap that needs further tightening

The system prompt contains keyword-sensitive routing instructions (e.g., 'when users mention subscription or account, gather customer information first') that override otherwise unambiguous tool descriptions
The model has a known bias toward customer tools on accounts-related vocabulary
Few-shot examples in the prompt accidentally bias the model toward get_customer
questions.rationale: When tool descriptions are confirmed unambiguous but a keyword consistently steers behavior in a specific direction, the source is almost always a system prompt instruction that reacts to that keyword. The fix is reviewing the prompt for routing language, not re-rewriting the already-good tool descriptions.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: The agent has finished gathering all available context. Which of the following situations genuinely warrants escalation to a human?
options: The customer is upset and using profanity, even though the request is a routine refund within policy
The customer's request — a partial refund for a defective item under warranty — falls clearly within documented policy

The customer requests a goodwill credit because of repeated shipping delays. Company policy covers refunds for damaged products but is silent on goodwill credits for shipping delays. The agent should escalate for policy interpretation
The customer is asking the same question for the third time but the documented answer hasn't changed
questions.rationale: Genuine policy gaps — where existing rules don't cover the situation and the agent would have to invent policy — are the textbook escalation case. Emotional intensity alone is not a reason if the path forward is clear. Re-explaining a documented answer doesn't require human judgment.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: In about 9% of refund cases, the agent processes a refund without first calling verify_account_owner, leading to refunds applied to the wrong customer when names collide. The verification step is in the system prompt as a 'must always' rule. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Add stronger language to the system prompt ('CRITICAL: NEVER skip verify_account_owner')
Add few-shot examples showing verify_account_owner being called first in every flow
Add a programmatic prerequisite in your tool layer that blocks process_refund from executing unless verify_account_owner has returned a verified result in the current session
Switch to a more capable model that follows instructions more reliably
questions.rationale: Critical business rules need deterministic enforcement, not probabilistic prompt instructions. A code-level prerequisite check makes skipping verification impossible regardless of LLM behavior. Stronger prompt language and few-shot examples reduce but cannot eliminate the failure rate.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent achieves 95% accuracy on single-issue requests but only 62% on requests that combine 2+ concerns ('refund my last order AND change my email AND extend my warranty'). What's the most appropriate first intervention?
options: Add 4–6 few-shot examples showing the correct decomposition and tool-call sequence for multi-concern requests
Block multi-concern requests at the input layer and force users to submit one issue at a time
Switch to a higher-tier model only for multi-concern requests
Add a system prompt rule saying 'handle one concern at a time'
questions.rationale: The agent handles each individual concern well; the gap is in how to decompose and route across multiple concerns in one message. Few-shot examples with worked reasoning are the highest-leverage, lowest-cost intervention for this kind of pattern-recognition gap. Blocking compound requests degrades UX.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Logs show the agent calls get_customer when users ask product availability questions, instead of lookup_inventory. The tool descriptions are both about one line long. What's the most cost-effective first step?
options: Expand each tool's description with input formats it accepts, example queries, edge cases, and explicit boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools
Restrict the agent's tool list to inventory-related tools when product keywords are detected
Train an embedding classifier to route requests before tool calls
Add a 'routing' tool the agent must call first
questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the LLM's primary input for selection. When descriptions are minimal and selection is unreliable, expanding them with concrete details (input formats, example queries, boundaries) is the highest-leverage first move. Embedding classifiers and routing tools add complexity for a problem that descriptions usually solve.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent's first-contact resolution rate is 51% — well below the 80% target. Reviewing escalations, you see that the agent escalates many cases that fall cleanly within standard return policy. What's the most proportionate first fix?
options: Lower the escalation rate by adding a hard limit on how many times per shift the agent can escalate
Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with few-shot examples that demonstrate when to escalate versus when to resolve autonomously
Remove the escalation tool entirely so the agent must resolve
Have a human review every case before it's classified
questions.rationale: The root cause is unclear decision boundaries. Explicit criteria plus few-shot examples directly teach the agent the boundary between 'resolve' and 'escalate' without adding infrastructure. Capping escalations or removing the tool punishes legitimate escalations alongside the over-eager ones.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent consumes two third-party MCP tools whose date formats vary: one returns ISO-8601, the other returns Unix epoch seconds. Logs show the agent occasionally misinterprets dates when comparing them across tools. What's the most maintainable fix?
options: Document the date formats in the system prompt and trust the LLM to convert
Add a PostToolUse hook that normalizes tool results (converts all timestamps to ISO-8601) before the agent processes them
Wrap each MCP server in a custom proxy that rewrites their output
Ask the upstream MCP authors to standardize their formats
questions.rationale: A PostToolUse hook gives you a deterministic, centralized point to normalize tool outputs in code before the agent reasons about them. This is uniform and maintainable. Prompt-based instructions are unreliable for type conversions; custom proxies add infrastructure; waiting on upstream changes is not under your control.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: On ambiguous requests like 'I have a question about my recent activity,' the agent sometimes calls get_customer when lookup_order_history is the more useful starting point. Tool descriptions are decent but not great. What's the most effective improvement?
options: Force the agent to always call both tools
Add 4–6 few-shot examples targeting the specific ambiguous cases, showing reasoning for why one tool was chosen over the plausible alternative
Add a 'recent activity' tool that calls both
Remove get_customer from this agent's tool list
questions.rationale: Targeted few-shot examples with explicit reasoning teach the model the comparative decision-making process it needs for edge cases — better than declarative rules. The examples address the exact ambiguity that's causing errors. Forcing both tools wastes calls; building a meta-tool adds complexity.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're implementing the agent loop. After each Claude API call, what is the canonical signal to decide whether to keep looping (execute tools and continue) or stop (return to the user)?
options: Count the number of tool calls in the response and stop at a fixed cap
Inspect the stop_reason field — continue when it equals 'tool_use', stop when it equals 'end_turn'
Parse the natural-language response for phrases like 'I'm done' or 'I need to call'
Track time elapsed since the request and stop after 30 seconds
questions.rationale: stop_reason is Claude's explicit, structured signal for loop control. 'tool_use' means Claude wants tools executed and results returned; 'end_turn' means Claude has finished. Parsing natural language or relying on arbitrary caps is brittle and breaks dynamic tool selection.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your get_customer tool returns multiple matches when searched by name alone (e.g., 'John Smith' has 14 matches). The agent currently picks the first one and proceeds, which causes a wrong-account error in roughly 17% of these cases. What is the most reliable mitigation?
options: Instruct the agent to always pick the most recent account
Have the agent ask the customer for an additional identifier (email, phone, or order number) before taking any customer-specific action
Prevent any action on accounts where the name has more than one match
Add a confidence score and proceed when confidence exceeds 80%
questions.rationale: The user holds the ground truth about their own identity. One extra conversational turn eliminates the error class entirely. Picking 'most recent' is a guess; blocking all multi-match accounts breaks legitimate flows; LLM confidence scores are not well calibrated for this kind of identity decision.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your support agent uses progressive summarization at 70% context capacity. After a few summarization rounds in long sessions, you see the agent recall amounts and order numbers incorrectly. What's the most effective fix?
options: Disable summarization and let the context overflow
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, IDs) into a persistent 'case facts' block included on every prompt, kept outside the summarized history
Increase the summarization threshold to 90%
Use a different model that's better at recall
questions.rationale: Summarization is inherently lossy for precise details. Pulling transactional facts into a structured persistent block — separate from the summarized history — ensures they are reliably available every turn regardless of summarization. The summary keeps the conversational shape; the facts block keeps the numbers exact.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're asked to add Stripe as a new payment provider to an app that already integrates with PayPal and bank transfers. There are at least three viable architectural approaches (a unified provider interface, a strategy pattern, or wrapping the existing PayPal adapter). Which mode is best?
options: Direct execution — just start writing code; you can refactor later
Plan mode — explore the integration options and their architectural implications, then present a recommendation before implementing
Run Explore subagent and immediately apply its recommendation
Have the user write a detailed spec first; do not start until the spec is approved
questions.rationale: Plan mode is for tasks with architectural implications and multiple viable approaches. It forces Claude to investigate, weigh trade-offs, and propose an approach before touching code. Direct execution would commit to one path blindly; mechanically applying Explore output skips the design step.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You want to create a custom /security-review slash command that the entire team can use, versioned with the repository. Where should the command file live?
options: In ~/.claude/commands/ on each developer's machine
In .claude/commands/ at the project root, committed to the repository
In a SECURITY.md file at the project root
In .claude/skills/security-review/SKILL.md
questions.rationale: Project-scoped commands live in .claude/commands/ at the project root. Because they're in the repo, every developer who clones or pulls automatically gets them. ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal commands; skills are a separate primitive with different semantics.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team's coding convention 'use Result<T, E> error types instead of throwing exceptions' has been applied consistently for months by the original developers. Three new hires joined and are getting code suggestions that throw exceptions instead. What's the most likely cause and fix?
options: The convention was committed but the new hires haven't pulled — have them run 'git pull'

The convention exists in the original developers' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level) instead of the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md. Move the instruction to the project-level file so all team members receive it
Claude has changed behavior between versions — update Claude Code on the new machines
Add a .claude/rules/error-handling.md with paths: ['**/*.rs']
questions.rationale: User-level CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) is private to each developer and is not version-controlled. The original developers' machines have the rule locally; the new hires' do not. Moving it to the project-level CLAUDE.md ensures every team member receives it automatically.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're tasked with extracting a 30-table reporting subsystem out of a monolith into its own service. Dependencies are tangled. What's the right approach?
options: Direct execution — just start moving files
Plan mode — explore the codebase, map dependencies, and design an extraction approach before any code changes
Ask Claude to delete the reporting code and rewrite it from scratch
Run only the Explore subagent without any planning phase
questions.rationale: Large architectural restructurings with tangled dependencies are the canonical plan mode case. Mapping dependencies and choosing service boundaries before modifying files is the difference between a clean extraction and an expensive rollback.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're building a /brainstorm-approaches skill that lets the team explore alternative implementations for a problem. Discussions tend to be verbose with many discarded ideas, and you don't want this noise in the main conversation context. What frontmatter option should the skill use?
options: context: fork — runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so exploration doesn't pollute the main conversation
context: shared — keeps everything visible in main context for transparency
allowed-tools: none
disable-model-invocation: true
questions.rationale: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context. The verbose exploration happens in the fork; the main conversation receives a summary. This keeps abandoned approaches and brainstorm content out of subsequent implementation work.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team wants to add a Linear MCP server for pulling issues and updating statuses. Each developer authenticates with their own personal Linear API token. What's the right configuration approach?
options: Each developer adds the server with their literal token in their own ~/.claude.json
The team commits a project-scoped .mcp.json that references the token via environment variable expansion (${LINEAR_TOKEN}); document the required env var in the README
Add the literal Linear token to the project .mcp.json so everyone gets the same config
Don't use a project .mcp.json at all; have each developer configure Linear in CLAUDE.md
questions.rationale: Project .mcp.json with environment variable expansion gives a single, version-controlled source of truth for the server shape while keeping each developer's token in their environment. The token never enters the repo. Literal tokens in .mcp.json expose credentials; CLAUDE.md is not a configuration file for MCP.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A teammate has created a /commit skill in .claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md that enforces team commit standards. You want a personal variant that adds an emoji prefix without disturbing your teammates. What's the right approach?
options: Edit the team's project skill to make the emoji optional
Create a personal version in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name like /my-commit
Add an environment variable that switches behavior
Override the project skill by creating an identically-named ~/.claude/skills/commit/
questions.rationale: Project skills take precedence over personal skills with the same name. To keep both available, use a different name (like /my-commit) in your personal ~/.claude/skills/ directory. The team's /commit stays intact for everyone.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You asked Claude Code to implement a function that converts incoming webhook payloads into a normalized internal event schema. The first three attempts wrote logically correct code but used the wrong field nesting and inconsistent timestamp formats. Prose descriptions of the schema aren't working. What's the most effective next step?
options: Add more emphasis to the prose description
Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples showing the expected transformation on representative payloads
Have Claude generate documentation for the schema and use that as the spec
Switch to a more capable model
questions.rationale: Prose descriptions are inherently ambiguous for structural transformations. Concrete input/output examples eliminate that ambiguity by showing exactly what the right answer looks like. This is the canonical refinement technique when the model interprets a description differently across runs.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your codebase has distinct conventions: GraphQL resolvers, REST handlers, and Jest test files — each scattered across many feature directories rather than being colocated. You want each convention applied automatically when relevant files are edited. What's the most maintainable configuration?
options: Put all the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md so they're always loaded
Place a CLAUDE.md file in every directory that contains GraphQL, REST, or test files
Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns (e.g., paths: ['**/*.test.ts'], paths: ['src/api/**/*.ts'])
Use Claude Code skills that are manually invoked when editing those files
questions.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob-pattern frontmatter applies conventions to files by type regardless of where they sit in the tree. Putting everything in CLAUDE.md bloats every conversation; duplicating CLAUDE.md per directory is unmaintainable when test files are scattered; manual skills miss when developers forget to invoke them.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team has a /deploy skill that generates Kubernetes deployment manifests. Three issues have come up: developers run it without arguments and get errors, results sometimes get tangled with unrelated prior conversation context, and the skill occasionally writes to files outside its intended scope. What configuration changes fix all three?
options: Add argument-hint frontmatter (for arg prompting), context: fork (for isolation), and restrict allowed-tools to file write operations only
Add disable-model-invocation: true so only manual invocation is allowed
Move the skill from .claude/skills/ to .claude/commands/
Add a wrapper script that runs pre-flight checks before invoking the skill
questions.rationale: Three distinct skill features map cleanly to the three issues: argument-hint shows required parameters during autocomplete, context: fork isolates execution from main conversation history, and allowed-tools restricts the tool surface so the skill cannot perform out-of-scope writes.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your /audit-codebase skill produces detailed analysis but the verbose output is filling up your main conversation context, making subsequent work slower and less accurate. The skill itself works correctly. What's the fix?
options: Reduce the verbosity of the skill's output
Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter so the analysis runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only a concise summary returns to the main conversation
Run the skill in plan mode
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/ instead of project-level
questions.rationale: context: fork is purpose-built for this. The verbose analysis lives in the sub-agent context and is discarded after; the main conversation gets only the summary. Reducing verbosity may lose analytical value; plan mode is for design phases, not analysis.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CLAUDE.md has ballooned to over 600 lines covering TypeScript style, React patterns, testing conventions, deployment notes, and API contracts. Conversations are getting slower and the model is dropping relevant rules. What's the best refactor?
options: Move everything into multiple skills and invoke each manually
Compress CLAUDE.md by deleting the least-used sections
Create separate markdown files in .claude/rules/, each covering one topic (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md)
Move everything to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md instead
questions.rationale: .claude/rules/ supports topic-specific rule files. Splitting the monolith into focused, smaller files improves maintainability and lets you use frontmatter to apply rules only where they're relevant. Deleting content loses information; manual skill invocation breaks always-on conventions.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're rolling out structured logging across a 200-file codebase. The work has three phases: (1) discover every logging call and categorize it, (2) design the unified format, (3) apply changes consistently. Phase 1 produces a lot of output. How should you allocate?
options: Run all three phases in one session for maximum context continuity
Use the Explore subagent for Phase 1 to isolate verbose discovery output and return a concise summary, then continue Phases 2 and 3 in the main conversation
Use plan mode for all three phases
Skip Phase 1 and let Claude discover patterns as it implements
questions.rationale: Explore is purpose-built for noisy discovery: it works in an isolated context with read-only tools and returns a summary, keeping the main session clean for design and implementation. Running discovery in the main session pollutes context for phases where you need precision.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CLAUDE.md has grown to 500 lines, mixing universal coding standards (always relevant) with task-specific workflows (PR reviews, deployments, database migrations). Each conversation pays the cost of loading workflow content that's only occasionally needed. What's the best reorganization?
options: Keep everything in CLAUDE.md but compress it
Move everything into skills and require manual invocation for all instructions
Keep universal coding standards in CLAUDE.md (always loaded) and move task-specific workflows into Skills with trigger keywords for on-demand invocation
Split CLAUDE.md into multiple files and use @import to load them all
questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md is always-on and should hold the conventions that apply to every conversation. Skills are on-demand and ideal for occasional workflows. The split mirrors the cost: pay always for things you always need, pay only when needed for things you use sometimes.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You've found that including 2–3 reference exemplar service implementations in context produces dramatically better quality when Claude generates new services. But you don't want those exemplars loaded for unrelated tasks like debugging or refactoring. What's the right configuration?
options: Always include the exemplars in CLAUDE.md
Create a skill that references the exemplar services and includes pattern-following instructions, invoked on-demand via a slash command when generating new services
Add the exemplars to .claude/rules/ with no path filter
Train a custom Claude model on the exemplars
questions.rationale: Skills are perfect for this: they're invoked on demand. The exemplars and pattern-following instructions ship together via the skill and load only when generating new services. CLAUDE.md would bloat every conversation; unfiltered rules would do the same.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated review flags 'comments that may be misleading.' Reviewers complain that the agent flags acceptable patterns like brief shorthand comments while missing comments that actually contradict the code. What's the most effective prompt change?
options: Add 'be more conservative' to the prompt
Replace the vague instruction with explicit criteria: flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the actual code behavior
Add a confidence threshold and only show high-confidence findings
Have a human review every comment flag before posting
questions.rationale: Vague instructions like 'misleading' or 'be conservative' don't constrain the model. Explicit, falsifiable criteria — 'comment claim contradicts code behavior' — give the model a precise definition that eliminates both false positives on acceptable patterns and false negatives on real issues.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A PR touches 18 files in a payments module. Your single-pass review produces inconsistent depth — some files get thorough feedback, others get superficial comments, and the same code pattern is flagged in one file but approved in another. What's the most effective restructuring?
options: Reject PRs larger than 10 files
Split the review into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow
Use a model with a larger context window to handle all 18 files at once
Run three independent passes on the full PR and only report issues that appear in 2+ runs
questions.rationale: Attention dilutes across many files in one pass. Per-file analysis ensures consistent depth for local issues; a separate integration pass catches cross-file concerns. Larger context windows don't fix attention distribution. Rejecting large PRs shifts the problem to developers.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated code review has wildly different false positive rates by category: security findings are 8% false positive, correctness findings 12%, but style findings are 58% false positive and naming findings 64%. Developers are dismissing all categories because of the noise. What's the right interim move?
options: Stop running automated review entirely until the false positive rate is below 5% overall

Temporarily disable the high false positive categories (style, naming, documentation) and run only the high-precision categories (security, correctness) while you improve prompts for the noisy categories
Lower the model temperature on style and naming categories
Auto-resolve all style and naming findings instead of posting comments
questions.rationale: Trust is the asset under threat. Removing noise immediately restores trust in the categories that still run, and gives you time to improve the others without the bad ones dragging down the whole system. Stopping everything wastes the precision of the high-quality categories.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You currently use real-time API calls for both pre-merge style checks (developers wait) and weekly architectural debt reports (run overnight). The manager wants to move both to the Message Batches API for 50% cost savings. How should you respond?
options: Switch both to batch with a timeout fallback to real-time
Use the Message Batches API only for the weekly architectural debt reports; keep real-time calls for pre-merge style checks where developers are blocked
Switch both to batch with status polling for completion
Keep real-time for both to avoid result-ordering issues with batch
questions.rationale: Batch has up to 24-hour processing time with no real-time SLA. That's fine for overnight reports but unacceptable for blocking pre-merge checks. Match each workflow to the right API. Polling, fallbacks, and 'often faster' don't make batch suitable for blocking flows. Result correlation is handled by custom_id.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You have two CI modes: a fast pre-merge style check (developer waiting, blocking), and a nightly comprehensive analysis (polls results in the morning). Which is the right candidate for the Message Batches API?
options: Both
The nightly comprehensive analysis only
The pre-merge check only
Neither — always use real-time for code reviews
questions.rationale: Nightly analysis is already overnight, tolerates latency, and uses a polling completion model — a perfect fit for the Batch API's async, poll-based design. Capturing 50% cost savings there has no downside. Pre-merge checks block developers and must use real-time.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated reviews surface valid issues but the format varies turn to turn — sometimes structured (file, line, severity, fix), sometimes prose paragraphs, sometimes terse one-liners. Developers complain it's hard to scan. What's the most effective way to get consistent format?
options: Add stronger instructions like 'ALWAYS output in this exact format'
Provide 3–4 few-shot examples showing the exact format you want: issue identified, code location, specific fix suggestion
Switch to a more capable model
Pipe the output through a post-processor that reformats it
questions.rationale: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistent output format when instructions alone fail. Three to four examples give the model a concrete pattern to mimic. Stronger prose instructions are still probabilistic; post-processors are a code-layer workaround when prompts can be made to do the job.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your code review uses an iterative loop: Claude analyzes a file, requests a related file via a tool call, gets it back, then refines its review. You'd like to move this to the Batch API for cost savings. Why does it fundamentally not work?
options: Batch results take too long to return for the iterative flow

The Message Batches API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request — the asynchronous, fire-and-forget model prevents executing tools mid-request and returning results for Claude to continue
Tool calls cost extra in the Batch API
Batch and real-time tools have different schemas
questions.rationale: Batch is async and fire-and-forget by design. There's no mechanism to pause, execute a tool, and return results mid-request. Any workflow that requires multiple rounds of tool invocation and continuation within a single logical interaction is incompatible with the Batch API.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your GitHub Actions step runs `claude "review the diff for security issues"` and the workflow hangs indefinitely. What change makes it work?
options: Add a timeout to the GitHub Action step
Add the -p flag: `claude -p "review the diff for security issues"`
Pipe the output through stdbuf
Increase the runner's memory allocation
questions.rationale: Without -p (or --print), Claude Code starts in interactive mode and waits for a user. The pipeline hangs because nothing supplies input. -p tells Claude Code to process the prompt and exit — the canonical non-interactive flag for CI/CD.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: After your automated review produces 9 findings on a PR, a developer pushes 2 follow-up commits that address most of them. The next review run reposts the same 9 findings without acknowledging the fixes. How should the review pipeline be changed?
options: Have the pipeline diff the new findings against the prior ones and only post deltas
Include prior review findings as context in the prompt, instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
Delete prior review comments before each run
Run the review only on the latest commit, not the full diff
questions.rationale: Including prior findings in context lets Claude reason about whether each one was addressed by the new commits. The model can naturally distinguish 'still present' from 'now fixed.' Pure string diffing misses cases where the fix changes how a finding manifests.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI/CD does three Claude-powered analyses: (1) quick style checks per PR (blocking developer), (2) weekly security audit, (3) nightly test-coverage analysis. Which mix of APIs makes sense?
options: Real-time API for all three
Batch API for all three to capture maximum savings
Real-time API for the per-PR style checks; Message Batches API for the weekly security audit and nightly test-coverage analysis
Real-time for the style and audit; batch only for the nightly coverage
questions.rationale: Match latency requirements to API choice. Per-PR style blocks developers → real-time. Weekly audits and nightly coverage have flexible deadlines that easily fit inside the batch processing window, capturing 50% savings on both.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated review averages 18 findings per PR. Developers report that triage is the bottleneck — investigating each finding takes too long, and you can't filter findings because every category occasionally produces real issues. What change helps without dropping findings?
options: Cap findings at 5 per PR by category
Require Claude to include its reasoning and a confidence assessment inline with each finding so developers can triage quickly
Move the review to a manual reviewer
Reduce the review's scope to security findings only
questions.rationale: Inline reasoning and confidence assessments accelerate triage without dropping findings. Developers can quickly skim and prioritize. Hard caps lose real issues; manual review doesn't scale; narrowing scope drops legitimate categories along with noise.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated review tags findings as critical / high / medium / low, but developers complain that similar issues get different severities across PRs. What's the most effective fix?
options: Remove severity tags entirely
Include explicit severity criteria in the prompt with concrete code examples for each severity level
Have a human re-tag every finding before posting
Lower temperature on the severity classifier
questions.rationale: Inconsistency comes from ambiguous severity definitions. Explicit criteria plus concrete code examples per severity give the model unambiguous reference points. Temperature affects randomness, not the underlying definition problem.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI runs Claude Code in --print mode for code review. You parse the natural-language output with regex to extract findings, which sometimes fails when the format varies. Posting inline PR comments requires file path, line number, severity, and suggested fix. What's the most reliable approach?
options: Add stricter prompt instructions like 'always return findings as a JSON array'
Use the CLI flags --output-format json and --json-schema to enforce structured output at the CLI level, then parse the structured_output field to post inline comments via the GitHub API
Switch to a more capable model so the natural-language output is more consistent
Run the review twice and only act on findings that match between runs
questions.rationale: CLI-level enforcement with --output-format json and --json-schema guarantees well-formed, schema-conformant output. Regex on natural language is fragile by design. Stronger prompt language is still probabilistic. The structured output appears in the structured_output field, not result.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated review generates test case suggestions when reviewing implementation changes. Developers complain that many suggested tests duplicate existing tests they already have. What's the simplest fix?
options: Filter suggested tests through a regex matcher against existing test files
Include the existing test file in the context so Claude can identify what scenarios are already covered before suggesting new ones
Limit the number of test suggestions per review
Have developers write tests first and review only the implementation
questions.rationale: Claude can only avoid suggesting already-covered scenarios if it knows what tests exist. Providing the test file in context is direct and effective. Regex matching is fragile (a test of the same scenario can be written many ways).
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You notice Claude-generated code suggestions are sometimes inconsistent: when the generator agent's reasoning is included in the review context, the review tends to approve flawed code that aligns with the original reasoning. What's the most effective change?
options: Have the generator agent self-review before submitting
Have a second, independent Claude Code instance review the changes without seeing the generator's reasoning
Increase the temperature on the review agent
Lengthen the review prompt with stricter rubrics
questions.rationale: Sharing the generator's reasoning creates confirmation bias in the reviewer — the same rationalization that produced the code also leads to its approval. An independent reviewer without access to that reasoning mirrors human peer review and catches issues the generator rationalized away.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A SaaS billing assistant currently loops indefinitely on complex disputes. The engineer writes: `while iterations < 5: response = call_claude(...)`. Production reports the agent stopping mid-resolution when it has clearly more work to do. What's the architectural flaw?
options: The iteration cap of 5 is too low for billing disputes
The loop terminator should be the stop_reason field — specifically continuing on tool_use and exiting on end_turn — not an arbitrary iteration count
The model should be configured with longer max_tokens per response
Billing disputes require a dedicated subagent rather than the main loop
questions.rationale: Iteration caps are safety nets to prevent runaway loops, not the primary control mechanism. stop_reason is Claude's explicit, structured signal: tool_use means continue, end_turn means done. Replacing structured control flow with a counter abandons the autonomous behavior the agent was built for.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your fraud-review coordinator delegates a transaction check to an analyzer subagent. The coordinator's prompt insists 'always quote dollar amounts in USD.' The subagent returns amounts in EUR for European transactions. Engineering blames the model. What's the actual fix?
options: Add the USD requirement as a few-shot example in the coordinator prompt
Switch to a larger model for the subagent
Forward the USD requirement explicitly in the Task tool payload sent to the subagent — subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history
Use a PostToolUse hook to convert currencies after the fact
questions.rationale: Subagents start blank. They see only what the Task tool payload contains. A constraint living in the coordinator's history is invisible unless forwarded. This is the canonical context isolation question.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A travel-booking agent runs the following plan: (1) get user preferences, (2) search flights, (3) search hotels, (4) check loyalty status, (5) build itinerary. Steps 2, 3, and 4 don't depend on each other. The current implementation runs them in sequence. What's the most cost-effective improvement?
options: Combine flight and hotel search into one tool to reduce call count
Emit Task calls for steps 2, 3, and 4 in the same coordinator turn so they execute as parallel subagents
Cache flight results to skip step 2 on repeat requests
Move steps 2-4 to the Message Batches API
questions.rationale: Independent steps belong in the same wave. The coordinator emits multiple Task tool calls in a single response and they run in parallel. Batch API is wrong for blocking workflows. Caching is orthogonal. Combining tools loses specialization.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your insurance claims agent must call verify_policy_holder before any payout. The rule is in the system prompt. Audit reveals 4% of payouts went out without verification during long conversations under context pressure. What's the most reliable fix?
options: Rephrase the rule with stronger language and uppercase warnings
Add few-shot examples showing the verified-before-payout sequence
Configure a PreToolUse hook on process_payout that blocks the call unless verify_policy_holder has returned a verified result in the current session
Have a separate Claude instance audit each payout decision
questions.rationale: Hard business rules need deterministic enforcement. Prompt instructions are probabilistic and degrade under context pressure. A prerequisite gate makes the violation structurally impossible.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A 30-step legal document review workflow crashed at step 22 after running for two hours. The team restarts and the agent begins again at step 1. What architectural change prevents this?
options: Switch to the Message Batches API for resilience
Increase the max_tokens cap so the agent can produce more output per call
Have each agent export its state after each completed step to a known location, and have the coordinator maintain a manifest that lets resume logic skip completed steps
Reduce the number of steps by combining them
questions.rationale: Crash-recovery manifests are a named exam pattern. Without them, crashed multi-agent workflows restart from zero. With them, each agent picks up where it left off, with findings and partial results intact. Batch API is the wrong tool entirely.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A coordinator partitions 'global supply chain resilience' into three subtopics: semiconductors, lithium, and rare earths. The final report comes back covering only those three materials, missing labor, shipping, and trade-policy dimensions of supply chain resilience. Where's the bug?
options: The subagents need access to more tools
The coordinator over-narrowed task decomposition — partitioning was too tight to cover the breadth of 'supply chain resilience'
The synthesis subagent dropped material
The web search subagent should have searched broader queries on its own initiative
questions.rationale: Granularity is the coordinator's call. Over-narrow decomposition guarantees coverage gaps even when every subagent performs correctly. Subagents executed exactly what they were asked; the upstream partition was the bug.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team proposes letting the document-analysis subagent call the web-search subagent directly when it needs to fact-check a claim. What property of the system are you giving up?
options: Token efficiency, since direct calls bypass the coordinator
Observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow, and a single chokepoint for policy enforcement
The ability to use the Message Batches API
Compatibility with the Claude Code CLI
questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke is the architectural property, not just a routing choice. Centralized communication is what gives you observability, consistent recovery, scoped context handoffs, and a single place to enforce policy. Direct subagent calls sacrifice all of those.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: During a customer chat, the user writes: 'Cancel my November subscription, refund the unused portion, and update my mailing address to my new place.' Your agent currently answers only the cancellation. What's the right architectural change?
options: Train the agent to detect compound messages and reject them with a 'one issue at a time' reply
Decompose the message into three distinct concerns, share customer context across them, investigate in parallel where independent, and synthesize a unified resolution
Process the first concern and ask the user to resend the others
Use a more capable model that handles longer inputs
questions.rationale: Multi-concern decomposition is a named Domain 1.4 skill. Decompose, share context, investigate in parallel where the steps don't depend on each other, then merge into one response. Rejecting compound requests degrades UX; serial handling burns tokens.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An incident-triage agent escalates a ticket because a customer is 'extremely angry and using harsh language' — but the actual request is a routine refund well within policy. The agent should not have escalated. What does this reveal?
options: The model is too cautious by default

The system prompt's escalation criteria are missing a clear principle: emotional intensity alone is not an escalation trigger; escalation triggers are policy gaps, explicit customer requests, or inability to progress
The agent needs a sentiment analyzer
Escalations should require human approval
questions.rationale: Escalation criteria must be explicit and tied to operational triggers (policy gaps, explicit requests, inability to proceed). Emotional tone is not a trigger if the path forward is documented and clear.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're modeling a research workflow as a DAG. fact_check consumes outputs from web_search and document_analysis. report_writer consumes outputs from fact_check. web_search and document_analysis have no dependencies. How many waves?
options: One — run everything in parallel
Four — one task per wave for determinism
Two — Wave 0: web_search + document_analysis (parallel). Wave 1: fact_check + report_writer
Three — Wave 0: web_search + document_analysis. Wave 1: fact_check. Wave 2: report_writer
questions.rationale: Wave 0 holds the independent tasks (web_search, document_analysis). Wave 1 has fact_check which depends on Wave 0. Wave 2 has report_writer which depends on Wave 1. Three waves. Option A ignores dependencies; B over-serializes; C miscounts by putting fact_check and report_writer in the same wave even though report_writer depends on fact_check.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your e-commerce agent calls 3 MCP tools that return timestamps in 3 different formats: created_at as Unix epoch, order_date as ISO 8601, and ship_date as 'MM/DD/YYYY HH:MM'. The agent occasionally compares dates incorrectly. What's the right fix?
options: Add a system prompt note explaining each tool's format
Configure a PostToolUse hook that normalizes all returned timestamps to ISO 8601 before the model sees them
Wrap each MCP tool in a custom proxy
Ask the MCP server maintainers to standardize
questions.rationale: PostToolUse hooks are built for this: deterministic normalization before the model reasons about the data. The MCP-specific field is updatedMCPToolOutput. Prompts cannot reliably overcome format drift.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A coordinator delegates code-quality review to a subagent. After running for an hour, the subagent's context fills with diff content and reasoning. Quality drops. What's the cleanest pattern?
options: Increase the subagent's max_tokens
Have the subagent return structured findings (file, line, severity, suggestion) instead of raw diff content plus reasoning, so the coordinator only receives compressed structured data
Switch to a larger model
Restart the subagent every 15 minutes
questions.rationale: Reduce token volume at the source. Structured findings preserve what the coordinator needs; raw reasoning chains and verbatim diff content inflate context without adding value.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An agent escalates to a human supervisor by attaching the full 47-turn chat transcript. The supervisor takes 12 minutes to read it before acting. What's the right handoff pattern?
options: Reduce the transcript to the last 5 turns
Compile a structured handoff package: customer ID, root cause, attempted actions, recommended next step, relevant policy references
Have the human read the transcript on a faster screen
Use the supervisor's existing context
questions.rationale: Structured handoff packages replace transcripts. Humans operating an escalated ticket need the decision-relevant facts up front, not the conversation. This is a named Domain 1.4 skill.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're choosing between two task decomposition strategies. Task A: 'review these 40 source files for security issues and produce a summary.' Task B: 'add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase nobody has documented.' Which fits which pattern?
options: Both are dynamic adaptive decomposition
Both are prompt chaining
Task A is prompt chaining (predictable per-file pass + cross-file pass); Task B is dynamic adaptive decomposition (plan emerges as the codebase is mapped)
Task A is dynamic; Task B is prompt chaining
questions.rationale: Prompt chaining suits predictable multi-aspect work with known steps. Dynamic adaptive decomposition is for open-ended investigations where you can't list subtasks in advance. Code review across known files → chaining. Test coverage of an unknown codebase → adaptive.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your sales agent uses a 50,000-token policy document on every interaction. Costs are spiraling. The CFO suggests batch processing. The agent is conversational and customers wait for responses. What's the right cost optimization?
options: Message Batches API for 50% savings
Prompt Caching — cache the 50K-token policy prefix; cache reads cost 90% less, cache writes have a 25% premium (5-min TTL); the math works as long as you read the cache more than you refresh it
Switch to a smaller model
Trim the policy document to the most common 5K tokens
questions.rationale: Batch API can't serve a live conversation. Prompt Caching is purpose-built for repeated static prefixes in user-facing flows: 90% read savings, 25% write premium. Trimming policy creates compliance risk; a smaller model degrades quality.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A coordinator that has been running for 90 minutes starts producing answers like 'based on typical refund patterns' instead of citing specific facts from earlier in the conversation. What's happening?
options: The model is hallucinating
Context degradation — earlier specific facts have been pushed into low-attention regions or compacted away, so the model is falling back to generic patterns
The system prompt is corrupted
The agent needs more tokens per call
questions.rationale: 'Referring to typical patterns instead of discovered specifics' is the named symptom of context degradation in extended sessions. The fix is scratchpad files for persistent fact storage and/or /compact to free attention.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You have two MCP tools. search_knowledge_base(query) returns dynamic results based on input. The 'customer reliability tier registry' is a static reference dataset agents can read by ID. Classify each:
options: Both Tools
search_knowledge_base as Tool, customer reliability tier registry as Resource
Both Resources
search_knowledge_base as Resource, customer reliability tier registry as Tool
questions.rationale: Tools execute and return computed/dynamic results. Resources are static data agents read by reference. If you can't run it, it's a Resource. The reliability registry is data; the search function is a verb.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent has these 14 tools: 6 for customer profile management, 4 for order/shipping operations, 4 for billing/refunds. Tool selection accuracy is at 71% and dropping. What's the structural fix?
options: Rewrite every tool description with more detail

Reduce the agent's tool count by splitting into specialized subagents — one for customer/profile, one for orders, one for billing — each holding only its 4-6 relevant tools, coordinated by a parent agent
Add a routing tool the agent calls first
Remove the least-used tools
questions.rationale: Tool counts above ~8 fragment the agent's attention regardless of description quality. The architectural fix is decomposition into specialized subagents with 4-6 tools each. Description rewrites cannot overcome attention fragmentation.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A developer puts a personal Notion API token into the project's .mcp.json for convenience. Why is this wrong?
options: It's not wrong — Notion supports shared tokens
.mcp.json is committed to source control, exposing the personal token in version history; either use environment variable expansion (${NOTION_TOKEN}) or place the personal server in ~/.claude.json
The .mcp.json format doesn't support authentication
Notion MCP requires user-scoped configuration only
questions.rationale: Project .mcp.json is committed; personal credentials must never be in it as literals. The two correct options: environment variable expansion to keep the shape committed without the secret, or move the personal server to ~/.claude.json.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your fetch_product_data MCP tool fails with a generic '"error": "operation failed"'. The coordinator retries 5 times, then escalates. Most failures were timeouts that would have resolved on retry. What's missing?
options: Better retry logic at the coordinator

The tool should return structured error metadata: errorCategory (transient/validation/business/permission), isRetryable boolean, and a human-readable description so the coordinator can make informed recovery decisions
Longer timeouts on each call
A circuit breaker after 3 failures
questions.rationale: Generic errors give the coordinator nothing to act on. Structured error metadata with category and retryability turns probabilistic recovery into deterministic routing. Retry logic alone can't distinguish transient from terminal failures.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You have a tool called process_data. Production shows it's being invoked with everything from images to PDFs to URLs. What's the cleanest fix?
options: Add input validation inside process_data to reject unsupported types
