Split it into purpose-specific tools with explicit input/output contracts (extract_text_from_pdf, extract_text_from_image, fetch_url_content), each with descriptions that include negative bounds ('does NOT handle...')
Add few-shot examples showing correct usage
Rename it to process_anything
questions.rationale: Generic tools invite generic usage. Splitting into purpose-specific tools with clear contracts and negative bounds eliminates the routing problem at the structural level. Validation only catches misuse after it's attempted.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Two MCP tools — summarize_article and summarize_document — have nearly identical descriptions. The coordinator misroutes 22% of requests. What's the primary fix?
options: Add a system prompt rule mapping content types to tools

Rename to differentiate (e.g., summarize_web_article and summarize_uploaded_document) and rewrite descriptions to state input format, expected output, and explicit negative bounds pointing to the sibling tool
Combine them into one tool with a source_type parameter
Add a routing classifier
questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism the model uses to select tools. Semantic overlap = misrouting. Rename to eliminate overlap, then add negative bounds. Combining loses specialization.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your coordinator must always call validate_request before submit_request. The team has tried adding it to the system prompt and adding few-shot examples. Production still skips validation 3-6% of the time. What's the correct deterministic mechanism?
options: Stronger language in the system prompt
A programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks submit_request until validate_request has returned a successful result in the current session
tool_choice: 'any'
Larger model
questions.rationale: Prompt-level guidance is probabilistic. Prerequisite gates make the violation structurally impossible. This is the Domain 1.4 / 2.3 pattern: deterministic enforcement for hard ordering rules.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You want to guarantee that an extract_invoice_metadata tool fires before the agent does anything else with the document. Which tool_choice setting works?
options: tool_choice: 'auto' — let the model decide
tool_choice: 'any' — force some tool, model picks
tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'extract_invoice_metadata'} — force a specific named tool
tool_choice: 'required' plus a system prompt mention
questions.rationale: Only the named-tool form guarantees a specific tool runs. 'any' forces some tool but the model picks; 'auto' is fully discretionary; 'required' isn't a documented value of the tool_choice field. System prompts are not deterministic.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An MCP server is set up to expose a database schema catalog so agents know what tables and columns exist before issuing queries. Should this be a Tool or a Resource?
options: Tool, because agents query it
Resource — it's a content catalog providing context, not a function that executes computation
Prompt template
It depends on whether the database supports indexing
questions.rationale: Catalogs of available data — schemas, source registries, document indexes — are Resources. They reduce exploratory tool calls by letting the agent see what exists before invoking tools. They don't execute; they're read.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A subagent encounters a transient API timeout. Currently every transient failure propagates immediately to the coordinator. The coordinator is spending most of its time orchestrating retries that the subagent could handle locally. What's the proper escalation discipline?
options: Always escalate every error for centralized visibility
Implement local recovery for transient failures within the subagent and propagate only what cannot be resolved locally, including what was attempted and any partial results obtained
Suppress all errors silently
Let the coordinator do all retries
questions.rationale: Errors should be handled at the lowest level capable of resolving them. Transient errors → retry locally. Unresolvable errors → escalate with attempt history and partial results so the coordinator has context.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An agent's search_internal_docs tool sometimes returns '0 results' for legitimate queries. The agent treats this identically to 'search service unreachable' and retries. What distinction is missing?
options: None — both are failures

'0 results' is a valid empty success indicating the query ran but found nothing; 'service unreachable' is an access failure requiring a retry decision. The tool should return distinct error categories so the coordinator can make appropriate routing decisions.
The tool should always return at least one result
The agent should default to fallback search
questions.rationale: Empty results and access failures are semantically different outcomes. Conflating them wastes retries on legitimately empty queries or treats real failures as complete. Structured error responses must distinguish them.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team uses Claude Code for backend work. Three new contractors join. They don't get the team's testing conventions in their suggestions. Existing team members do. What's the most likely cause?
options: The contractors are on a different Claude Code version
The conventions live in original developers' ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level) instead of the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md (project-level, committed) — the new contractors never receive them
The contractors need to run /init
The conventions belong in .claude/rules/
questions.rationale: User-level CLAUDE.md is private to each developer. Conventions that apply to the whole team must live in the project-level file so they're committed and automatically available to anyone who clones.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your codebase has Python files in services/, TypeScript files in web/, and test files (.test.ts, _test.py) scattered everywhere. You need test files to follow specific conventions regardless of directory. What configuration approach fits?
options: Put a CLAUDE.md in every directory that contains tests
Create .claude/rules/testing.md with YAML frontmatter paths: ['**/*.test.ts', '**/*_test.py'] so the conventions apply when editing any matching file
Put all test conventions in the root CLAUDE.md
Use a Skill that contractors invoke manually before editing tests
questions.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob path frontmatter is built for cross-directory conventions. Root CLAUDE.md loads on every conversation regardless of relevance; per-directory CLAUDE.md is unmaintainable when files are scattered; manual skill invocation is fragile.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: What two Shift+Tab presses cycle Claude Code into?
options: default → auto → plan
default → acceptEdits → plan
default → plan → acceptEdits
default → readOnly → plan
questions.rationale: Permission modes cycle default → acceptEdits → plan. Two presses from default reaches plan mode. Auto mode is a separate opt-in feature available only on certain plans (Max/Team/Enterprise/API), not part of the default cycle.

questions.text: A 90-minute Claude Code refactoring session is running long. The main session's context is filling with verbose grep results, file dumps, and exploration output. The actual refactor is stalling. What's the right move?
options: Restart the session
Use the Explore subagent for additional discovery — it runs read-only in its own isolated context (Haiku by default) and returns a summary, freeing the main session's context for the refactor work
Increase the model's max_tokens
Switch to plan mode
questions.rationale: Explore is purpose-built for offloading verbose discovery. It's read-only (denied Write/Edit), runs on Haiku by default for speed and cost, and returns a summary. Plan mode keeps everything in the main session. Restarting burns the actual refactor work in progress.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You want a /release skill that requires a --version argument, runs in isolation from the main conversation, and can only write to specific files (no destructive operations). What frontmatter combination?
options: argument-hint: '--version <semver>', context: fork, allowed-tools: ['Write', 'Edit']
disable-model-invocation: true
context: shared, auto-approve: true
paths: ['**/CHANGELOG.md']
questions.rationale: argument-hint prompts for required parameters during autocomplete; context: fork isolates the skill's execution from the main conversation; allowed-tools restricts the tool surface. Three separate features, each mapped to one of the three requirements.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A team-shared /changelog skill exists in .claude/skills/changelog/SKILL.md. You want a personal variant that adds extra metadata, available only to you, without affecting the team. What's the right approach?
options: Edit the team skill in the project repo
Create a personal variant under ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name (e.g., /my-changelog) — project skills take precedence over personal skills with the same name, so a unique name is required
Put the variant in .claude/skills/ with the same name
Modify your local CLAUDE.md to override the skill
questions.rationale: Project skills win against same-named personal skills. The only way to keep both available is to use a different name in your personal skills directory.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A CI runner executes `claude "review this diff for SQL injection vulnerabilities"`. The pipeline times out. The same prompt works on developer laptops. What's the minimal fix?
options: Add a --timeout flag
Add the -p (or --print) flag so Claude Code runs non-interactively and exits after processing
Run the CI step in a tty
Install a different Claude Code version on the runner
questions.rationale: Without -p, Claude Code starts in interactive mode and waits for a user. The CI runner provides no interactive input, so the process hangs. -p is the canonical non-interactive flag for CI/CD usage.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI pipeline needs Claude Code's review output as JSON with specific fields (file, line, severity, suggestion). The current `claude -p "review ..."` returns natural language. You're using regex to parse it and it's fragile. What's the proper approach?
options: Write better regex
Use --output-format json and --json-schema '{...}' — the output appears in the structured_output field as schema-validated JSON
Add 'always return JSON' to the prompt
Use a smaller model that's more predictable
questions.rationale: CLI-level enforcement with --output-format json plus --json-schema guarantees structurally correct output. Prompt-based JSON instructions are probabilistic. Note: structured output appears in the structured_output field, not result.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI runs Claude Code in Docker. Behavior is inconsistent across machines because developers' local configs (skills, hooks, MCP servers, CLAUDE.md files) leak into the container's auto-discovery. What flag fixes this?
options: --isolated
--bare — skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, giving reproducible CI behavior
--no-config
--clean
questions.rationale: --bare is the Anthropic-recommended CI flag for reproducibility. Documentation notes it will become the default for -p in a future release. The complete recommended pattern is claude --bare -p 'prompt'.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Claude is asked to refactor a function and produces three iterations, each interpreting your prose description slightly differently — wrong field names one time, wrong return type another. What's the most effective refinement technique?

Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples showing the expected transformation on representative cases, eliminating prose ambiguity
Switch to plan mode for the refactor
Use a larger model

questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team uses Claude Code to migrate from Express to Fastify across 80+ files. Three integration approaches are viable with different infrastructure implications. The team disagrees on which to pick. Which mode?
options: Direct execution — start writing code and refactor later
Plan mode (Shift+Tab twice) — Claude maps dependencies, weighs trade-offs across the three approaches, and presents a recommendation before any file modification
The Explore subagent alone
Use a custom slash command
questions.rationale: Multiple viable approaches, architectural implications, and large-scale changes are the canonical plan mode case. Plan mode forces investigation and strategy before code modification. Explore is for noisy discovery; direct execution would commit blindly.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your project CLAUDE.md is at 750 lines covering five major topic areas. Conversations are slow and the model occasionally misses applicable rules. Each conversation pays the cost of loading all 750 lines. What's the cleanest refactor?
options: Compress with shorter wording
Move universal coding standards into CLAUDE.md and split task-specific workflows (deployments, migrations, PR reviews) into skills that load on-demand via slash commands
Move everything into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Delete the least-used sections
questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md is always-on; skills are on-demand. Universal conventions go in CLAUDE.md; occasional workflows go in skills. The split aligns load cost with usage frequency.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A data extraction pipeline uses 'Always respond with JSON only, no extra text' in the system prompt. 12% of outputs include markdown fencing or explanatory prose. What's the durable fix?
options: Make the instruction more emphatic
Add few-shot examples of raw JSON
Use tool_use with a JSON schema for programmatic enforcement at the API layer — the structural guarantee replaces the probabilistic suggestion
Switch to a more capable model
questions.rationale: Prompt-based JSON instructions are always probabilistic. The exam consistently rewards programmatic enforcement via tool_use with schemas, or --output-format json / --json-schema at the CLI level. Few-shot reduces but doesn't eliminate failures.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your invoice extraction occasionally fabricates a value for the purchase_order_number field on invoices that don't include one. The schema marks the field as required. What's the fix?
options: Add a prompt instruction to leave it blank when missing
Mark the field as nullable/optional in the JSON schema so the model isn't forced to fabricate a value to satisfy a required constraint
Switch to a larger model
Add validation to reject extractions without PO numbers
questions.rationale: A required field with no source data forces the model to choose between schema violation and fabrication. Making the field nullable eliminates the pressure to hallucinate. This is a named Domain 4.3 skill.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A validation-retry loop in your extraction pipeline retries with the message 'Your previous output was invalid. Please try again.' Over half the retries fail identically. What's missing?
options: More retries
The retry message must include specific feedback identifying which field failed validation and what's expected — generic messages give the model no new information to correct on
A different model on retry
Lower temperature on retry
questions.rationale: Validation-retry loops only converge when feedback is specific. 'Field total failed: expected number, got one hundred dollars' guides correction; 'invalid, try again' is no signal at all.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI runs a nightly test-generation job over 5,000 source files. Each invocation is independent and there's no human waiting until morning. Which API serves this best?
options: Synchronous API
The Message Batches API — 50% cost savings, fits the up-to-24-hour processing window, uses custom_id to correlate request/response pairs
Prompt Caching only
Real-time API with rate limiting
questions.rationale: Batch is purpose-built for non-blocking, latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads. Overnight test generation fits perfectly. custom_id is how you correlate responses back to inputs.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your code review needs an iterative loop: Claude analyzes a file, requests a related file via tool call, gets it back, refines the review. You'd like to use Batch API to save 50%. Why does it fail?
options: Batch results take too long

The Message Batches API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request — it's asynchronous and fire-and-forget, with no mechanism to execute tools mid-request and return results for Claude to continue
Tool calls cost extra in Batch
Tool schemas differ between Batch and real-time
questions.rationale: Batch is fundamentally async. Any workflow requiring multi-turn tool calling within one logical interaction is incompatible. This is a named exam fact.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Severity ratings produced by your automated code reviewer vary across PRs. The same null-check omission is flagged 'medium' one day and 'high' another. What's the fix?
options: Lower model temperature
Include explicit severity criteria in the prompt with concrete code examples for each severity level so the model has unambiguous reference points
Use a larger model
Average severities across multiple runs
questions.rationale: Inconsistency in classification flows from ambiguous criteria. Explicit definitions plus concrete examples give the model unambiguous anchors. Temperature affects randomness; criteria affect calibration.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your review pipeline produces 20+ findings per PR. Developers say triage is slow because every finding requires investigation to assess. You can't filter findings (every category occasionally has real issues). What's the proportionate fix?
options: Cap findings at 5 per PR
Require Claude to include reasoning and confidence assessment inline with each finding so developers can triage at a glance
Have a human review every finding
Reduce to only security findings
questions.rationale: Inline reasoning and confidence assessments accelerate triage without dropping findings. Caps lose real issues; humans don't scale.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A code-review system flags many 'comments may be misleading' findings. Reviewers report that many flags are normal shorthand comments that aren't misleading at all. What's the prompt fix?
options: 'Be more conservative'
Replace the vague criterion with a falsifiable one: 'flag a comment only when its claimed behavior contradicts the actual code behavior'
Add a confidence threshold
Lower temperature
questions.rationale: 'Misleading' is subjective; 'contradicts actual code behavior' is testable. Falsifiable criteria reduce false positives at the prompt layer.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You want consistent output format from a model but instructions alone produce variation. What technique is most effective?
options: Stronger imperative language
3-4 few-shot examples showing the exact format you want
Higher temperature
Lower max_tokens
questions.rationale: Few-shot examples are the canonical technique for format consistency. Stronger language is still probabilistic. The exam explicitly tests this preference.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A 14-file PR review produces inconsistent depth — detailed feedback on some files, superficial on others, contradictory comments where identical patterns are flagged in one file and approved in another. What's the fix?
options: Reject PRs larger than 10 files
Split into focused passes: per-file local analysis, then a separate cross-file integration pass — this matches the prompt-chaining decomposition pattern for predictable multi-aspect work
Use a larger context window
Add few-shot examples
questions.rationale: Attention dilutes across many files in one pass. Per-file passes ensure consistent depth; a separate integration pass catches cross-file concerns. Larger context windows don't fix attention distribution.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're parsing the output of `claude -p "review" --output-format json --json-schema "{...}"`. Where does the schema-validated content appear in the JSON response?
options: In the result field
In the structured_output field — regular text output appears in result, but schema-constrained output is placed in structured_output
In content[0].text
In the output field
questions.rationale: This is a frequently-tested distinction. Plain output goes to result; schema-constrained output goes to structured_output. Parsing the wrong field is a common pipeline bug.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your code generator and code reviewer are both Claude instances. The reviewer often approves flawed code from the generator. What's the architectural fix?
options: Have the generator review its own output more carefully
Use a second independent Claude instance for review without access to the generator's reasoning context — eliminates the confirmation bias inherent in self-review
Add extended thinking to the reviewer
Use a larger reviewer model
questions.rationale: Self-review retains the original decision-making context, biasing the reviewer toward approving. Independent instances without the generator's reasoning catch issues the generator rationalized away. Extended thinking doesn't fix this; bias does.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your long-running coordinator's context has filled past 70% capacity. Progressive summarization runs, but on the next several turns the agent recalls order totals incorrectly — confusing $1,847 with $1,487. What's the fix?
options: Disable summarization
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, IDs) into a persistent 'case facts' block included on every prompt, separate from the summarized history
Move to a larger context window model
Increase summarization aggressiveness
questions.rationale: Summarization is inherently lossy for precise details. Persistent fact blocks anchor exact values outside the summarized history. Larger context windows don't change attention distribution.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A 30K-token input shows good attention at the start and end but poor mid-section coverage. The model misses key data buried in the middle. What's this called?
options: Context overflow
Token truncation
The 'lost in the middle' effect — attention is strongest at the beginning and end of context; mid-section content receives less attention regardless of total context size
Recency bias
questions.rationale: 'Lost in the middle' is the named attention distribution pattern in transformer LLMs. Larger windows don't fix it. The mitigation is structural: place critical information at edges, use headers, prime with summaries at the top.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A document-extraction pipeline self-reports a confidence of 0.91 on every output. The team wants to use this to skip human review on high-confidence cases. What discipline should they apply first?
options: Trust the scores at the 0.91 threshold and reduce review immediately

Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled validation set — map model confidence to actual accuracy so you can defend the routing threshold (e.g., '0.85 confidence = 92% actual accuracy on this document type')
Lower the threshold to 0.85 for safety
Use a single universal threshold across all field types
questions.rationale: Raw self-reported confidence is uncalibrated. Field-level confidence calibrated against a labeled validation set is a legitimate routing signal; raw confidence is not. This is a named Domain 5.5 skill.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your extraction pipeline reports 97% accuracy overall. Customer complaints come in for credit memos specifically. What measurement discipline catches this?
options: Increase the overall accuracy threshold to 99%
Stratified random sampling and accuracy analysis broken down by document type and field — aggregate accuracy hides poor performance on specific segments (e.g., 99% on invoices, 73% on credit memos)
Increase sample size for overall accuracy
Add more validation rules
questions.rationale: Aggregate metrics hide local failure. Stratified sampling and per-segment accuracy reveal which document types and fields are actually performing well. Raising the overall bar doesn't help if the bad segments are dominated by good ones.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Two credible sources in a synthesis report different unemployment numbers. The synthesizer flags this as a contradiction. Investigation reveals the sources are from different months. What metadata pattern prevents this in future?
options: Use only one source per topic
Require subagents to include publication or data-collection dates in structured outputs, so the coordinator can recognize temporal evolution rather than treating it as contradiction
Always pick the more recent source
Use LLM judgment to reconcile
questions.rationale: Conflicting statistics are often temporal differences, not contradictions. Date metadata in structured outputs distinguishes the two cases. Without dates, the coordinator can't tell.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your research synthesis flattens everything into prose paragraphs: financial comparisons, news narratives, and lists of technical findings all read the same way. Readers complain it's hard to find data. What's the fix?
options: Make the prose more detailed
Render content appropriately for its type: financial data as tables, news narratives as prose, technical findings as structured lists — uniform formatting destroys signal in presentation
Use bullet points everywhere
Add more headings
questions.rationale: Content-type-appropriate rendering is a named Domain 5.6 skill. A financial comparison rendered as prose hides the numbers; a news narrative rendered as a table strips its context.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your customer support deployment has Zero Data Retention (ZDR) compliance requirements. The team proposes using the Message Batches API for overnight ticket analysis to save 50%. Why is this wrong?
options: ZDR doesn't apply to ticket analysis
The Message Batches API is not eligible for Zero Data Retention — use the real-time API even for non-blocking workloads when ZDR compliance is required
Ticket analysis can't be done overnight
The 50% savings only applies to real-time calls
questions.rationale: ZDR ineligibility for Batch API is a named CCA exam fact. When ZDR is required, the synchronous API is the only option even for non-blocking workloads. The cost optimization that remains is Prompt Caching.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A pipeline processes 50K tokens of static policy context plus a small variable user message per request. The user is waiting on each response. Costs are too high. What's the right cost optimization?
options: Batch API for 50% savings
Prompt Caching — cache reads cost 90% less, cache writes cost 25% more on 5-minute TTL; for high-throughput repeated prefixes the read savings dominate the write premium
Smaller model
Reduce the policy context
questions.rationale: Live user-facing workflows can't use Batch. Prompt Caching is the cost optimization for repeated static prefixes with users waiting. The economics work when reads dominate writes.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your sequential 8-step compliance workflow runs for 90 minutes. Step 6 crashed last night and the team had to restart from step 1, losing all completed work. What pattern provides durability?
options: Add retry logic to step 6

Each step exports its output to a known location (manifest file or key-value store); on resume, the coordinator loads the manifest, identifies which steps completed, and resumes from the next pending step rather than restarting
Add longer timeouts
Run on a faster machine
questions.rationale: Crash-recovery manifests are the named CCA pattern for durable multi-step workflows. Without them, every crash restarts from zero. The manifest is structured state on disk, not chat-history reconstruction. Retries and timeouts address symptoms, not durability.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A junior engineer reviewing your agent loop asks why you don't just check whether the assistant's last text contains the phrase 'I'm done' to decide when to stop iterating. What's the correct response?
options: Phrase matching is fine as long as you also lowercase the response first
Loop termination should be driven by the API's stop_reason field; parsing prose is fragile and conflates a presentation artifact with a control signal
You should check for an empty content block instead of a phrase
Use a regex with multiple variants of 'done' to make it robust
questions.rationale: stop_reason is the structured signal Claude exposes for exactly this purpose: tool_use means continue, end_turn means stop. Reading the prose to guess intent is the textbook anti-pattern.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A research coordinator briefly mentions in turn 4 that 'all citations must be peer-reviewed.' In turn 11, it spawns a literature subagent that returns blog posts and preprints. Engineering files a bug against the subagent model. What's actually wrong?
options: The subagent ignored the peer-review constraint and needs a stronger prompt
The constraint never reached the subagent because subagents start with an empty context; the coordinator must include 'peer-reviewed only' inside the Task payload it sends
The literature subagent needs a different model variant
The coordinator should run the subagent twice and reconcile
questions.rationale: Subagent context does not inherit. Whatever lives in the coordinator's conversation history is invisible to the spawned subagent unless it's bundled into the explicit task payload.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A new architect on your team draws a diagram where the report-writer subagent calls the web-search subagent directly to grab a missing source mid-write. They claim this 'saves a round trip.' Which production property does this design lose?
options: Output token efficiency, because direct calls skip the coordinator's prompt overhead
A single chokepoint for observability, policy enforcement, and consistent error handling — the value of hub-and-spoke is not routing efficiency but architectural control
Compatibility with the Claude Agent SDK Task tool
The ability to run subagents in parallel waves
questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke is a control discipline, not a performance optimization. Once subagents call each other, you lose central visibility, central recovery, and central enforcement. Direct calls feel cheaper and cost you the architecture.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An onboarding agent runs these steps for a new hire: (1) fetch HR profile, (2) provision email account, (3) provision Slack account, (4) provision GitHub seat, (5) compile a welcome packet from all four. Steps 2, 3, and 4 don't depend on each other but currently execute serially. What's the appropriate restructuring?
options: Replace the four steps with one combined 'provision_all_accounts' tool
Have the coordinator emit Task calls for steps 2, 3, and 4 in the same turn so they run as a parallel wave, then proceed to step 5 once all three return
Cache the HR profile so step 1 is faster on subsequent runs
Move the whole flow to the Message Batches API
questions.rationale: Independent steps in the same logical phase belong in one wave: a single coordinator turn emits multiple Task calls that execute in parallel, then the next turn synthesizes. Combining tools loses specialization and observability.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your medical-records agent must run a PHI redaction tool before any external email is sent. The system prompt has said so for months. An audit found that under long conversations, the redaction step is skipped roughly 2% of the time. What's the durable fix?
options: Move the rule from the system prompt into a user-message reminder injected each turn
Add a PreToolUse hook on send_external_email that rejects the call unless redact_phi has produced a verified result earlier in the same session
Have a second model audit each outbound email after the fact
Rephrase the rule with stronger 'CRITICAL' formatting
questions.rationale: Probabilistic instructions degrade under context pressure. A prerequisite hook converts a soft rule into a structural one: the bad sequence becomes unreachable instead of merely discouraged.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A regulatory filing pipeline runs 18 sequential validation steps over four hours. Last week a transient cloud issue killed it at step 14 and the team had to re-run the whole pipeline. Which architectural pattern eliminates this category of waste?
options: Implement automatic retries with exponential backoff inside each step

Have each step persist its outputs and write its completion status to a manifest the coordinator reads on startup; on resume, completed steps are skipped and execution continues from the first incomplete step
Move the entire pipeline to the Message Batches API for inherent durability
Reduce the step count by combining adjacent validators
questions.rationale: A manifest plus persisted step outputs is the canonical crash-recovery pattern for multi-step workflows. Retries can't recover from a process crash; combining steps trades robustness for fragility; Batch API isn't a control-flow tool.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A research coordinator was asked to assess 'the state of small modular reactors.' It split the work into four subagents covering Westinghouse, NuScale, Rolls-Royce SMR, and X-energy. The final report covers vendor profiles thoroughly but misses regulatory landscape, fuel supply, and grid-integration concerns. Diagnose the failure.
options: The subagents under-performed on their assigned vendors
The synthesis subagent dropped material between its input and its output
Decomposition was too narrow — splitting by vendor rather than along dimensions of 'state of SMRs' guaranteed coverage gaps regardless of how well each subagent executed
The coordinator should have run more vendor subagents
questions.rationale: Granularity is a coordinator decision. Splitting into four vendor slices structurally precludes coverage of cross-cutting topics. The subagents did their jobs; the partition was the bug.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A support agent escalated a refund ticket because the customer's message contained three exclamation marks and the word 'ridiculous.' The refund itself was clearly within standard policy. What does this case point to?
options: The agent's escalation logic conflates emotional intensity with operational criteria; the rule should escalate on policy gaps, explicit human requests, or inability to proceed — not on customer sentiment alone
The system needs a separate sentiment-analyzer tool
All refund decisions should require human approval as a safety net
The model is too conservative and should be tuned to be more aggressive
questions.rationale: Escalation triggers must be operational and explicit. Emotional tone is not a reason to escalate when the path forward is policy-clear. Adding sentiment tooling reinforces the mistake instead of fixing it.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Model a research workflow as a DAG: collect_raw_data and review_literature have no dependencies. clean_data depends on collect_raw_data. statistical_analysis depends on both clean_data and review_literature. write_report depends on statistical_analysis. How many parallel waves are required?
questions.rationale: Wave 1: collect_raw_data + review_literature (parallel, no deps). Wave 2: clean_data. Wave 3: statistical_analysis. Wave 4: write_report. Four waves total; the longest dependency chain determines the wave count, not the number of nodes.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent's conversation history is approaching the context window limit. The team proposes simply truncating the oldest messages every turn. What's the principal risk this creates that a structured summary plus a persistent facts block avoids?
options: Truncation is fine for short-context models but breaks larger ones

Truncation evicts arbitrary facts the agent may still need (verified IDs, escalation history, prior commitments), causing silent regression; structured summarization plus a stable facts block preserves what's load-bearing while shrinking what's narrative
Truncation slows the API calls because of cache misses
Truncation requires recomputing the system prompt
questions.rationale: Naive truncation is information-blind and removes content by position, not by relevance. The disciplined alternative compresses narrative history and pins precise facts in a stable block.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A startup is consolidating four customer-facing agents (returns, billing, shipping, account changes) into one large agent with all 18 of their tools merged together. The lead engineer believes this is simpler. What's the predictable outcome on the exam's expected design grounds?
options: It simplifies deployment and is generally preferred
Tool selection accuracy will degrade as the tool count grows past the 5-to-8 range; the system loses the structural advantage of attention-scoped specialists coordinated by a hub
It's fine as long as tool descriptions are short
It improves latency because the agent skips one delegation hop
questions.rationale: The super-agent anti-pattern is named on the exam: one over-armed agent loses tool selection accuracy as the surface grows. Specialized subagents with 4-to-6 tools each, coordinated by a hub, is the preferred shape.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A user writes: 'Move my next delivery to a hold, refund the duplicate charge from last Tuesday, and change my preferred contact to email.' Your agent currently responds to only the delivery change. What's the right structural fix?
options: Train the agent to detect compound requests and ask the user to send them one at a time
Decompose the message into three concerns up-front, fetch shared customer context once, handle independent concerns in parallel, then synthesize a single combined response
Process them serially in the order they appear, asking the user to confirm between each
Switch to a larger model that handles longer inputs better
questions.rationale: Multi-concern decomposition is the named pattern: identify each concern, fetch shared context once, fan out on independent work, then merge. Splitting the conversation degrades UX; serial handling burns tokens duplicating customer lookups.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A coordinator dispatches three parallel subagents. Two return clean results; the third hits a credentials error and aborts. What's the appropriate hub-and-spoke behavior?
options: The coordinator should immediately abort the whole request because partial results are dangerous
The coordinator receives the structured error from the failing spoke, decides whether to retry, degrade, or surface a gap; the two successful results are not discarded just because a sibling failed
The successful subagents should retry their own work until the failing one recovers
The successful subagents' results should be cached and the coordinator should silently restart
questions.rationale: Each spoke fails or succeeds independently. The coordinator is the place that decides what partial completion means for the user request: retry, degrade gracefully, or report the gap. Siblings do not retry on each other's behalf.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Two hours into a Claude Code refactor session, the agent starts using generic naming conventions instead of the specific patterns it correctly applied at the start of the session. It also begins re-discovering files it already read. What's happening and what's the right intervention?
options: The model has been downgraded mid-session; restart with a different model

Context degradation — specific facts have been pushed into low-attention regions or compacted; the appropriate intervention is to persist the load-bearing facts (style rules, file inventory) into a scratchpad referenced by the next prompt, and run /compact
The agent needs more tokens per response
The CLAUDE.md file was deleted
questions.rationale: 'Reverting to generic patterns' and 'forgetting earlier specifics' are the textbook symptoms of context degradation in long sessions. The fixes are persistent scratchpads for facts plus compaction for noise.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An engineer proposes routing live customer-support chat traffic through the Message Batches API to cut costs by 50%. Why is this fundamentally wrong?
options: Batch responses can exceed 24 hours and customers are waiting on each turn; Batch fits non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads, not interactive ones
Batch API doesn't support tool use of any kind
Batch outputs are charged at a premium when used with tools
Batch can't be combined with system prompts
questions.rationale: Batch trades latency for cost: results may take up to 24 hours. Anything where a user is waiting is incompatible. The right fit is overnight or back-office processing where no one is blocked.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your multi-agent research system reliably gets the first synthesis pass roughly 80% complete. The remaining 20% requires targeted re-querying — a small set of unresolved gaps that an iteration could close. The current design hands the first synthesis directly to the user. What's the missing step?
options: Add a larger context window to the synthesis agent

Insert a coordinator-level evaluation step that inspects the first synthesis for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries to the relevant subagents, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient — this is the named iterative-refinement loop
Have the synthesis agent score its own confidence and stop only when above 0.95
Run two synthesis agents in parallel and average their outputs
questions.rationale: Iterative refinement at the coordinator level is the named pattern: the coordinator owns the gap-evaluation step, not the synthesis agent. Self-scored confidence is uncalibrated; averaging duplicate outputs doesn't close coverage gaps.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your MCP server exposes (a) get_invoice_pdf(invoice_id) which retrieves a specific PDF, and (b) a curated list of the company's 50 approved compliance templates that agents should read from before drafting. Classify (a) and (b):
options: Both are Tools
(a) is a Tool because it executes a retrieval with an input parameter; (b) is a Resource because it's a static, addressable content set the agent reads as reference material
(a) is a Resource, (b) is a Tool
Both are Resources because they both return data
questions.rationale: Tools execute and produce computed outputs from inputs. Resources are addressable static content the agent reads. 'Retrieval that runs and returns a specific result' is a tool; 'a catalog the agent can browse' is a resource.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Two tools, search_help_articles and search_internal_wiki, have similar descriptions ('search documentation for relevant content'). Your agent picks the wrong one 30% of the time. Which fix attacks the root cause first?
options: Add a routing classifier upstream of the model

Rewrite both descriptions to specify input format, expected return shape, and an explicit negative bound pointing to the sibling tool ('does NOT search the internal wiki; use search_internal_wiki for that')
Combine them into a single search tool with a parameter for the source
Add a system-prompt rule that maps query keywords to tools
questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary input to selection. Semantic overlap causes misrouting. Disambiguating descriptions with negative bounds — 'does NOT cover X' — is the canonical fix. Combining loses specialization.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your fetch_supplier_record tool returns the literal string 'error' on failure. The coordinator can't tell whether the supplier ID was malformed, the supplier exists but the database is briefly unreachable, or the agent lacks permission. What's missing?
options: The tool should retry internally before failing

Structured error metadata: a category (validation, transient, permission, business), an is_retryable flag, and a human-readable detail so the coordinator can route recovery deterministically instead of guessing
A circuit breaker after N consecutive failures
Longer timeouts on every call
questions.rationale: Opaque error strings force the coordinator to retry blindly. Categorized errors let it distinguish 'fix your input' from 'try again later' from 'you can't do this' without trial and error.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A developer commits a .mcp.json that contains a literal personal Notion token. The repo is public on the company GitHub. What's the appropriate corrective action?
options: Rotate the leaked token, then either reference it via environment variable expansion (e.g. ${NOTION_TOKEN}) in .mcp.json, or move the personal server config out to ~/.claude.json so it's never committed
Add the .mcp.json to .gitignore and leave the existing commit alone
Restrict the token's scope in Notion and re-commit
Replace the literal token with a placeholder string and re-commit
questions.rationale: Project .mcp.json is committed. Personal secrets must never live there as literals; environment-variable expansion keeps the shape committed without the secret, and per-user config in ~/.claude.json is the alternative. The leaked token must also be rotated — gitignore doesn't undo history.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your pipeline must guarantee that an extract_metadata tool runs as the first action on every uploaded document. Which tool_choice setting accomplishes this with the strongest guarantee?
options: tool_choice: 'auto' with a system-prompt instruction
tool_choice: 'any' so the model is forced to call some tool
tool_choice: {type: 'tool', name: 'extract_metadata'} — the named-tool form is the only configuration that forces a specific tool
tool_choice: 'required' combined with a few-shot example
questions.rationale: Named-tool selection is the only setting that forces a specific tool. 'any' forces a call but lets the model pick; 'auto' is fully discretionary; 'required' isn't a documented value of this field.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Production logs show a do_data_thing tool being invoked with image URLs, raw CSV strings, and natural-language questions. It works sometimes and fails unpredictably. What's the clean refactor?
options: Make do_data_thing's description more detailed so the model uses it more carefully
Decompose it into purpose-specific tools (extract_csv_rows, summarize_image, answer_table_question) each with explicit input contracts and explicit negative bounds pointing at the others
Add input validation so do_data_thing rejects anything it doesn't recognize
Rename it to handle_data so the agent treats it as a fallback
questions.rationale: Generic tools invite generic — and wrong — usage. The structural fix is decomposition with contracts. Validation only catches misuse after it's attempted; a more detailed description on a generic tool can't make the generic surface specific.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: An agent's search_orders tool returns the same error code whether the search succeeded with zero matches or the orders service is offline. The agent retries both. What discipline is missing?
options: The agent should always try a fallback search before retrying

The tool should return two distinct outcomes — an empty success that says 'query ran, no matches' and a transient access failure that flags the service as unreachable — so the coordinator's routing logic can act on each correctly
The tool should never return zero results; it should fabricate a default match
The agent should call the tool twice and compare
questions.rationale: An empty result is a successful query with no hits. An access failure is a failed query. Conflating them wastes retries or hides real outages. Distinct outcomes let the coordinator make different decisions.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your single agent has accumulated 16 tools (5 for inventory, 6 for orders, 5 for returns). Tool-selection accuracy has dropped from 92% to 70%. The team's instinct is to rewrite every description in more detail. What's the better structural move?
options: Add a router tool the agent calls first to pick a category
Decompose into three specialized subagents — inventory, orders, returns — each holding only its 5-6 tools, coordinated by a hub; description rewrites cannot fix attention fragmentation past ~8 tools
Remove the four least-used tools
Switch to a larger model that handles more tools natively
questions.rationale: Past roughly 8 tools, the model's attention starts splitting across the surface no matter how well each description is written. The structural fix is specialization: smaller per-agent tool sets, coordinated centrally.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your data agent issues exploratory queries against a warehouse to figure out which tables and columns exist before running its real query. Each session wastes 4-6 calls on discovery. Which MCP primitive solves this?
options: A Tool called describe_schema that runs introspection on every session
A Resource that exposes the schema catalog as static, addressable reference content the agent reads once before issuing queries
A Prompt template that hard-codes the schema in the system prompt
A larger model so the agent guesses the schema correctly
questions.rationale: Catalogs of available data — schemas, source registries, document indexes — are Resources. Agents read them as context; they don't run them. Replacing exploratory tool calls with a readable catalog is the canonical use case.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A subagent's API client is hitting transient 503s on roughly 7% of calls; the coordinator escalates each one to a human operator. The on-call team is overwhelmed by retry tickets that would have resolved on a single retry. Which discipline correctly assigns recovery responsibility?
options: Always escalate every failure so the human team has central visibility

Implement local retry-with-backoff for the transient category inside the subagent; escalate to the coordinator only when local recovery fails, and include the attempt history and any partial results in the escalation
Have the coordinator perform retries on the subagent's behalf
Suppress 503s silently and continue with empty results
questions.rationale: Errors should be handled at the lowest level capable of resolving them. Transient failures recover locally with backoff. Unresolvable failures escalate upward with structured context so the coordinator has something to act on.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your agent calls two third-party MCP tools: one returns dates as ISO-8601 strings, the other as Unix epoch seconds. The agent occasionally compares them as strings, producing wrong orderings. What's the maintainable architectural fix versus relying on prompting?
options: Tell the agent in the system prompt to be careful about date formats
Normalize both tools' date fields to a single canonical format at the MCP-server adapter layer before they reach the agent, so the agent never sees a heterogeneous date representation
Add a third tool that converts between formats and instruct the agent to use it
Lower temperature so the agent makes fewer mistakes
questions.rationale: Prompt-level cautions are probabilistic. Normalizing at the adapter layer makes the failure mode structurally impossible: the agent only ever sees one format. Adding a conversion tool punts the problem back into prompt-following.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A senior engineer keeps the team's 'always run pre-commit hooks' rule in their personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Three new contractors joined and don't follow this rule. Where should the rule live and why?
options: In the senior engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — they should onboard contractors manually
In the project's .claude/CLAUDE.md, which is committed to the repo and automatically loaded for anyone who clones the project — user-level files are private to each developer
As a Skill in ~/.claude/skills/ that contractors invoke before each commit
In a README.md the contractors are expected to read
questions.rationale: Project-level CLAUDE.md is the right home for team-wide rules. User-level CLAUDE.md is private to a developer; it never reaches teammates or new hires.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your monorepo has Python in services/, TypeScript in web/, and Go in cli/, with Terraform files (.tf) scattered through services/ and infra/. You want Terraform-specific style rules to apply only when editing .tf files, anywhere they live. What's the right configuration?
options: Put the Terraform rules in the root CLAUDE.md
Create .claude/rules/terraform.md with YAML frontmatter paths: ['**/*.tf'] so the rule loads only when a matching file is in scope
Drop a CLAUDE.md into every directory that contains .tf files
Write a /terraform-style Skill the developer invokes manually before editing
questions.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob frontmatter is purpose-built for cross-directory, file-type-scoped conventions. Root CLAUDE.md is always-on and inflates every conversation; per-directory CLAUDE.md doesn't scale to scattered files; manual invocation is unreliable.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Starting from the default permission mode, how many Shift+Tab presses does it take to enter plan mode?
options: One
Two — the cycle is default → acceptEdits → plan
Three — the cycle is default → acceptEdits → readOnly → plan
Plan mode isn't reached by Shift+Tab; it's reached by a slash command
questions.rationale: The permission-mode cycle is default → acceptEdits → plan. Two Shift+Tab presses from default reaches plan. Auto mode is a separate opt-in feature not in the default cycle.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Halfway through a long refactor, your main Claude Code session's context is being eaten by verbose grep output and file dumps from exploratory questions. The refactor itself is stalling. What's the appropriate move?
options: Restart the session and re-explain the refactor
Increase max_tokens so the model can output more per response
Use the Explore subagent for further discovery — it runs read-only in its own context (Haiku by default) and returns a summary, freeing the main session for the refactor
Switch the main session into plan mode
questions.rationale: Explore is purpose-built for offloading noisy discovery. It runs read-only (Write/Edit denied), uses a faster model by default, and surfaces only a summary. Plan mode keeps the noise in the main session; a restart loses the in-flight refactor work.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You're designing a /publish-release Skill with three requirements: (1) it must require a --tag argument before running, (2) its execution must not pollute the parent conversation's context, (3) it must only be allowed to call git, gh, and Write tools — no shell or destructive operations. Which frontmatter combination matches all three?
options: argument-hint: '--tag <version>', context: fork, allowed-tools: ['git', 'gh', 'Write']
disable-model-invocation: true, paths: ['**/RELEASE.md']
context: shared, auto-approve: true, allowed-tools: ['*']
argument-hint: '--tag <version>', model: 'claude-haiku', read-only: true
questions.rationale: Three concerns map to three frontmatter fields: argument-hint enforces the required argument at autocomplete time; context: fork isolates the Skill's execution from the parent; allowed-tools whitelists exactly the tools needed.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team has a /test-fixture Skill at .claude/skills/test-fixture/SKILL.md. You want a personal variant with extra debug logging, just for you, without affecting teammates. Putting your version at ~/.claude/skills/test-fixture/SKILL.md doesn't work — your variant never runs. Why?
options: Skills only load from project directories
Project Skills take precedence over personal Skills with the same name; to keep both available, give yours a different name (e.g., /test-fixture-debug)
Skills with the same name in different directories are merged together
The ~/.claude/skills/ path is reserved for built-in Skills
questions.rationale: Same-name collisions resolve in favor of the project Skill. The clean fix is a unique personal name so both Skills coexist without overriding each other.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A GitHub Actions step runs `claude "audit this PR for hardcoded secrets"` and the workflow hangs forever. The same command works on a developer laptop. The minimal change?
options: Add `-p` (or `--print`) so Claude Code runs non-interactively and exits when finished
Add a `--timeout` flag
Run the step under a pseudo-TTY
Switch to a smaller model that responds faster
questions.rationale: Without -p, Claude Code starts in interactive mode and waits for a user. CI runners have no interactive input, so the process hangs. -p is the canonical non-interactive flag.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI runs Claude Code in Docker, but build results are inconsistent across machines because each developer's local hooks, Skills, and CLAUDE.md files leak into the image and influence auto-discovery. What single flag isolates the run?
options: --clean
--isolated
--bare — skips auto-discovery of hooks, Skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, giving deterministic CI behavior
--no-config
questions.rationale: --bare is the Anthropic-recommended CI flag for reproducible behavior. The documentation notes it's the basis for a future default in -p mode. The recommended pattern is claude --bare -p '...'.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI parses Claude Code's review output with regex and the parser breaks on roughly 1 in 8 runs because the format varies. You need findings as JSON with fields file, line, severity, fix. What's the durable approach?
options: Strengthen the regex and add more fallback patterns
Use `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema '{...}'`; the schema-validated result appears in the structured_output field of the JSON response, not in the natural-language result field
Append 'always respond with JSON' to the prompt and parse the entire response as JSON
Switch to a smaller, more predictable model
questions.rationale: CLI-level schema enforcement is structural and replaces probabilistic prompt-following. Note the parsing detail: schema-constrained output appears in structured_output, while plain text remains in result — a common pipeline bug.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your team is migrating an authentication subsystem from a homegrown JWT solution to either Auth0 or AWS Cognito. The change spans 60+ files and the two paths have different infrastructure and security trade-offs. Which Claude Code mode should drive the early stage?
options: Direct execution against the most experienced engineer's preference

Plan mode — Claude maps dependencies, evaluates the two paths against the codebase's current shape, and presents a recommendation before any file modification; the cost of starting work in the wrong direction here is high
The Explore subagent on its own
A custom /migrate Skill
questions.rationale: Multiple viable approaches, architectural implications, and large blast radius are the classic plan-mode case. Plan mode separates investigation and design from execution, which is exactly the discipline this change requires.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: You've asked Claude to write a function that maps incoming webhook payloads into your internal event schema. The first three attempts disagree on field nesting and timestamp formatting. More prose instructions aren't converging. What's the most effective next step?
options: Re-emphasize the requirements with capitalized warnings
Provide 2-3 concrete input → output examples of the transformation that exhibit the desired nesting and timestamp shape; concrete examples eliminate the prose ambiguity that's causing the drift
Switch to a larger model
Set temperature to 0 and hope for determinism
questions.rationale: Concrete examples are the canonical fix when prose-based instructions produce inconsistent code. They communicate exact shape without the ambiguity natural language carries.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your /architecture-audit Skill correctly produces a thorough analysis, but its 4000-line output keeps polluting the main conversation's context, slowing subsequent work in the session. The Skill logic is correct. What's the fix?
options: Make the Skill's output more concise
Set context: fork in the Skill's frontmatter so it executes in an isolated context and returns only a summary to the parent conversation
Run the Skill less often
Increase the main session's context window
questions.rationale: context: fork is the frontmatter option that isolates Skill execution from the parent's context window. The parent receives only the Skill's final result, not the full discovery noise.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your invoice-extraction service prompts the model 'Return ONLY valid JSON, no markdown.' Despite this, 9% of responses include ```json fences or trailing commentary, breaking the downstream parser. What's the durable fix?
options: Use even stronger prompt language with multiple capitalized warnings
Add 3 more few-shot examples of bare JSON output
Define the output as a tool with a JSON schema and use tool_use to enforce the shape at the API layer — programmatic structure replaces probabilistic prompt-following
Post-process the response with a regex that strips fences
questions.rationale: Prompt-level JSON instructions are always probabilistic. Tool_use with a schema is the structural enforcement layer. Few-shot reduces but doesn't eliminate the failure; regex post-processing is brittle.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your contract-extraction agent occasionally invents a value for renewal_clause on contracts that have no renewal clause. The field is marked required in the schema. Why does the agent fabricate?
options: The model is overconfident and needs lower temperature

A required schema field with no source value puts the model in a no-win position between schema violation and fabrication; making the field nullable lets it return null and removes the pressure to invent
The few-shot examples don't include enough negative cases
The schema needs a stricter type constraint
questions.rationale: Required-but-absent is the canonical fabrication trigger. Schemas should reflect reality: fields that may legitimately be missing should be nullable so the model has a valid way to say 'not present.'
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your extraction pipeline retries failed outputs with the message 'Output was invalid, please correct.' Across 800 retries last week, the corrected output failed again roughly 60% of the time. What change makes retries converge?
options: Allow more retries (currently capped at 2)
Use a different model on retry
Make the retry message specific: identify which field failed, what was expected, what was received — the model has no signal to correct on without specifics
Lower temperature on retry
questions.rationale: Validation-retry loops only converge when the feedback is actionable. 'Field total_amount: expected number, received "one hundred dollars"' guides correction; 'invalid' is no signal at all.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your finance team runs a nightly summarization job over 12,000 monthly reports. Results are reviewed the following morning. Which API minimizes cost?
options: The Message Batches API — purpose-built for non-blocking, latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads, with about 50% cost savings against real-time; custom_id correlates each response to its input
The real-time synchronous API for predictable latency
Prompt Caching alone, calling the real-time API with a cached prefix
A smaller, cheaper model on the real-time API
questions.rationale: Overnight processing with no human waiting is the textbook Batch case. Up to 24-hour processing window, ~50% savings, custom_id for correlation. Real-time pays a premium you don't need.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your data-cleanup workflow has Claude analyze a record, call a tool to fetch a related record, and then refine its decision based on both. You want to move it to the Batch API for 50% savings. Why is this incompatible?
options: Batch results take longer than 24 hours

Batch is asynchronous and fire-and-forget: there is no mechanism to execute a tool mid-request and return its result for the model to continue reasoning within the same Batch entry — multi-turn tool-calling requires the synchronous API
Batch API charges extra for tool calls
Tool schemas differ between Batch and real-time
questions.rationale: Batch is fundamentally async. Any workflow that needs the model to receive a tool result and continue the same logical interaction is incompatible. It's a named exam fact.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your automated code reviewer flags 'tests that look fragile.' Half the flags are normal happy-path tests. The reviewers say 'fragile' is too vague. What's the appropriate prompt fix?
options: Lower the model temperature so the reviewer is more conservative

Replace the vague criterion with a falsifiable one such as 'flag a test only when it depends on the system clock, the current working directory, or non-deterministic ordering' — testable criteria reduce subjective false positives
Add a confidence threshold to filter low-confidence flags
Increase the prompt's emphasis on 'be conservative'
questions.rationale: Subjective adjectives invite inconsistent classification. Falsifiable, observable criteria give the model unambiguous anchors. This is a named Domain 4.1 skill.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your code review surfaces 22 findings per PR. Developers complain that triage is the bottleneck because every finding requires investigation. You can't drop categories — each has occasional real issues. What change helps without losing findings?
options: Cap findings at 8 per PR
Require Claude to attach a brief reasoning line and a calibrated confidence score to each finding so developers can dismiss low-confidence items at a glance instead of investigating every one
Have a human review every finding before posting
Reduce review to security findings only
questions.rationale: Inline reasoning and confidence accelerate triage without dropping findings. Caps lose real issues; humans don't scale; restricting categories hides real defects.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your code generator and code reviewer are both Claude instances. The reviewer is given the generator's full reasoning trace as context. You observe the reviewer approving subtly flawed code that aligns with the generator's stated rationale. What's the architectural fix?
options: Add extended thinking to the reviewer
Use a larger reviewer model
Have the reviewer run as an independent instance without access to the generator's reasoning — withholding the rationale eliminates the confirmation bias that's causing the false approvals
Have the generator self-review its output before submission
questions.rationale: Sharing the generator's rationale primes the reviewer to agree. Independent instances without the original reasoning catch issues the generator already rationalized away. Extended thinking and bigger models don't fix bias.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: A 22-file PR review produces inconsistent depth — detailed feedback on the first few files, increasingly shallow on later ones, and the same anti-pattern flagged in file 2 but approved in file 18. What's the right restructuring?
options: Reject PRs over 10 files
Increase the model's context window

Decompose the review: run a focused per-file pass (uniform depth) followed by a separate cross-file integration pass that looks at patterns across files; this aligns the prompt-chaining decomposition with the multi-aspect work
Add few-shot examples for each file type
questions.rationale: Attention dilutes across many files in a single pass. Per-file passes ensure consistent depth; a separate integration pass catches cross-file concerns. Larger windows don't redistribute attention.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your model returns the same content in inconsistent shapes turn to turn — sometimes a paragraph, sometimes a bulleted list, sometimes a one-liner. Instructions alone aren't converging. What's the standard technique?
options: Stronger imperative language
Set max_tokens lower
Provide 3-4 few-shot examples that demonstrate the exact shape you want — examples are the canonical mechanism for format consistency
Switch to a model with deterministic outputs
questions.rationale: Few-shot examples are the standard technique for format calibration. They communicate shape without the ambiguity prose carries, and they're cheap to maintain alongside the prompt.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your CI pipeline parses `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema '...'` output and reads response.result, but the schema-validated content isn't there. Where should it look?
options: response.content[0].text
response.output
response.structured_output — schema-constrained content is placed in this field, separate from the natural-language result field
response.tool_use[0].input
questions.rationale: A frequently tested distinction: plain output goes to result; schema-constrained output goes to structured_output. Parsing the wrong field is a common pipeline bug.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your customer-facing assistant sends a 40K-token static policy preamble plus a tiny user query on each call. Traffic is heavy and users are waiting. Batch API isn't viable. What's the right cost lever?
options: Reduce the policy preamble by aggressively trimming it
Use Prompt Caching: cache reads are ~90% cheaper, cache writes are ~25% more expensive on a 5-minute TTL, so high-throughput repeated prefixes pay back the write premium quickly
Use a smaller model and ignore quality loss
Use the Batch API anyway for the policy portion
questions.rationale: Interactive workloads can't tolerate Batch's async latency. Prompt Caching is the cost lever for repeated static prefixes with users waiting. The economics work when read volume dominates write volume.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your support agent runs progressive summarization at 70% context. In long sessions, the agent now sometimes recalls the wrong order ID or transposes digits on dollar amounts. What's the right discipline?
options: Disable summarization and accept the context growth
Move to a model with a larger context window so summarization isn't triggered

Extract precise transactional facts (IDs, amounts, dates) into a 'case facts' block that is included verbatim on every prompt, separate from the summarized narrative history — summarization is inherently lossy for precise tokens
Increase summarization aggressiveness so the model relies on it less
questions.rationale: Summarization is fine for narrative context and brutal for precise tokens. Pinning load-bearing facts in a stable block — outside the summary — protects the values that must remain exact.
questions.source: Rick Hightower — Intent Solutions CCA-F practice exams (reuse granted 2026-07-21)

questions.text: Your 40K-token document review consistently catches issues at the start and end of the document but misses problems in the middle third — even when the same problem is obvious to a human reading the same section. What's this called?
options: Token truncation

The lost-in-the-middle effect — transformer attention is strongest at the beginning and end of context; mid-document material gets weaker coverage regardless of total window size, and the mitigation is structural placement of critical content at the edges
Context overflow
Recency decay
questions.rationale: Lost-in-the-middle is the named attention-distribution pattern. Larger windows don't change the shape of the curve. The fix is structural: place critical content at edges, use headers, and prime with top-of-context summaries.
